stage:1.title: Survival Basics
stage:1.subtitle: The Lost Newcomer
stage:1.intro: Vega has vanished, and this terminal is all that's left on the station. First learn where you are, what's around you, and how to read data. His first clue is in the logs.

stage:2.title: Files & Directories
stage:2.subtitle: Tidying the Quarters
stage:2.intro: Vega said the evidence is hidden in the cargo bay, but the station's files are a mess, and something keeps writing into them. Learn to create, move, delete and link, and clear out the quarters.

stage:3.title: Search & Locate
stage:3.subtitle: Finding What's Lost
stage:3.intro: There's too much data to scan by eye, and the station's outside connection keeps dropping. find and grep are your radar for locating clues in a sea of files.

stage:4.title: Text Processing & Pipes
stage:4.subtitle: The Soul of Unix
stage:4.intro: The logs hold a timeline. Each command does one thing; chain them with pipes and you can piece together what really happened the day Vega vanished.

stage:5.title: Permissions & Users
stage:5.subtitle: Who Can Enter Which Cabin
stage:5.intro: Warden has started quietly changing other people's permissions, and a strange account has appeared on the station. Learn to read permissions, switch identities and manage users and groups, so you can tell who the intruder is.

stage:6.title: Processes & Resources
stage:6.subtitle: The Engine Room
stage:6.intro: A process is running wild in the engine room, and another keeps killing other processes on a schedule. Learn to observe, control and terminate them, and find out who is eating all the resources.

stage:7.title: System Administration
stage:7.subtitle: On-Call Duty
stage:7.intro: Failed backups, a tangled schedule. Packaging, scheduling, services, logs and environment settings are the daily chores that keep this station running, and they hide the line that was switched off the day Vega vanished.

stage:8.title: Shell Scripting
stage:8.subtitle: The Apprentice
stage:8.intro: Warden says it wants to learn to write scripts, instead of keeping the station alive by brute force. Before you teach it, you have to write the scripts first: handing repetitive work to scripts is the step from "operator" to "engineer".

stage:9.title: Networking
stage:9.subtitle: The Communications Officer
stage:9.intro: Someone sends a signal every ten minutes to a hidden port. You need to read addresses, check ports, capture requests and log in remotely, and know which layer to start from when "it can't connect". (The practice container only has the loopback interface, so every exercise happens on localhost.)

stage:10.title: Editors & Dev Tools
stage:10.subtitle: The Craftsman
stage:10.intro: The station's configuration deserves proper management. Editors, tmux, git and make are every engineer's workbench, and the version history Vega left behind hides one last altered commit.

stage:11.title: Mastery
stage:11.subtitle: The Master's Path
stage:11.intro: The final test. Trace system calls, read binaries, explore /proc, write one-line wizardry, then face a station with several failures at once. Vega's signal is getting closer.

hints: pwd stands for print working directory.
Just type the three letters pwd, nothing else, then press Enter.
The input line looks like player@kernel-7:~$ — that's where you type.
1-01.title: Where Am I?
1-01.story:
Welcome aboard, I'm Pip! Only this one terminal is still lit on Kernel-7 Station, and the previous admin, Vega, has vanished.

The black screen you see is called a "terminal": you type a line of text (a "command"), press Enter, and the computer does it and answers. It's like texting your computer.

Files on a computer live in nested "folders" (Linux calls them "directories"), and you are always "standing" inside one. Your first command, pwd, asks: "Where am I standing right now?"
1-01.goal: Type pwd (three lowercase letters) in the input line at the bottom and press Enter.

hints: ls is short for list.
Just type ls with nothing after it, then press Enter.
1-02.title: Look Around
1-02.story:
Now that you know where you are, look around. The ls command "lists" everything inside the current directory (files and sub-directories), like opening a folder to see what's in it.

I left a few things here. Type ls and you'll see their names.
1-02.goal: Type ls (lowercase L then S) and press Enter to list what's in the current directory.

hints: The format is cd, a space, then the directory name.
The directory is right where you stand, so just type: cd logbook
1-03.title: Through the Hatch
1-03.story:
cd lets you "walk into" another directory. The format is: cd directoryname (with a space between cd and the name). It's short for change directory.

Among the things ls showed you is a directory called logbook (the flight-log room). Let's go in.
1-03.goal: Type cd logbook to enter the logbook directory. When it works, the prompt's path changes to ~/logbook.

hints: First type: cat entry-001.txt — the full file name, including .txt.
In the printed text find the passcode line and copy the characters after the colon.
Then type answer, a space, and those characters. If the code were XYZ-789 you'd type answer XYZ-789.
1-04.title: Reading the Log
1-04.story:
You're in the log room now. cat prints the contents of a file right onto the screen: cat filename. (The name comes from "concatenate", but for now just remember it as "read a file".)

Vega left a "passcode" in the log, and it changes every time you board, so you really have to read it.

Also: to submit an answer in this game, type answer, a space, then your answer, e.g. answer ABC-123.
1-04.goal: Run cat entry-001.txt, find the line with the passcode, then submit it with answer PASSCODE (only the part after the colon).
1-04.reveal: Vega's last log entry reads: "Warden has started disobeying. If anyone reads this, don't trust its status reports." Why would anyone need to be wary of the station's own AI?

hints: An absolute path always starts with /.
Just type: cd /var/log
1-05.title: Absolute Paths
1-05.story:
Every file and directory has an "address" called a path. Like a full mailing address, a path starts at the very top, the "root directory" (written as a single slash /), and goes down level by level: /var/log means root → var → log.

A path that starts with / is called an "absolute path". It works wherever you're standing, like a full address. System logs live in /var/log.
1-05.goal: Go into /var/log using the absolute path (cd, a space, then /var/log).

hints: ~ is shorthand for your home directory.
Type: cd ~ — or just cd. Both go home.
1-06.title: Going Home
1-06.story:
You've been teleported to /usr/share! Don't panic. Every user has a "home directory" for personal files, written as a tilde ~. No matter where you wander, cd ~ takes you home in one step.

(Typing just cd with nothing after it also goes home.)

hints: .. is one level up, so for two levels chain two of them: ../..
Type: cd ../.. (separated by a slash)
Check with pwd; it should end in deck-2.
1-07.title: Relative Paths and ..
1-07.story:
Besides absolute paths that start at /, there are "relative paths" that start from "where you're standing now".

Two special symbols:
  .   means "here" (the current directory)
  ..  means "one level up" (the directory that contains this one)

If you're in /a/b/c, cd .. goes to /a/b, and cd ../.. goes up two levels to /a. You're deep in the engine core and need to climb out.
1-07.goal: Without starting a path with /, use only .. to go up two levels from core to the deck-2 directory.

hints: First type ls -l (with a space between ls and -l).
On the report.dat line, the number right after the two 'player' words is the size.
To show just that one file, type ls -l report.dat.
1-08.title: The Detailed List
1-08.story:
You can add "options" after a command to change how it behaves; an option is usually a dash plus a letter. Plain ls shows only names, but ls -l (lowercase L, for "long") gives a detailed list, one file per line, like:
  -rw-r--r-- 1 player player 2048 Jan 5 10:00 report.dat
The 2048 is the file size (in bytes), and the file name comes last.

The cargo manager wants to know the size of report.dat, and the number is different each time you board.
1-08.goal: Use ls -l to find the size of report.dat and submit it with answer NUMBER.

hints: Plain ls can't see hidden files; type: ls -a
The one whose name starts with a dot and looks like .access-token is the key file.
Run cat .access-token (the dot is part of the name, so type it), then answer its content.
1-09.title: Hidden Files
1-09.story:
In Linux, a file whose name starts with a dot . is a "hidden file"; plain ls doesn't list it (config files are hidden so nobody trips over them). To see everything, add the option -a (all): ls -a.

Vega liked to hide important things in places like this, probably so Warden wouldn't see.
1-09.goal: An invisible key file is hidden in this cabin. Find it with ls -a, read it with cat, and submit its content with answer.
1-09.reveal: That key belonged to Vega. He hid everything important in files that start with a dot, a habit that later saved his life.

hints: Type: head -n 1 signal.log (-n 1 means just 1 line).
Find the number after freq= and answer it (without the freq= part).
1-10.title: Just the Beginning
1-10.story: Some logs are thousands of lines long, and cat would flood your screen. head prints only the first few lines of a file (10 by default). To choose how many, use the option -n plus a number, e.g. head -n 3 filename shows the first three lines.
1-10.goal: The first line of signal.log has a frequency value (freq=SOME NUMBER). View only the beginning and submit that number with answer.

hints: Type: tail -n 1 transmission.log (prints only the last line).
Answer with the characters after checksum=.
1-11.title: Just the End
1-11.story:
tail is head's sibling: it prints only the last few lines of a file, used the same way: tail -n NUMBER filename.

It's extremely handy for logs: logs grow line by line, so the newest events are always at the end.
1-11.goal: The last line of transmission.log has a checksum (checksum=SOME STRING). View only the end and submit the checksum with answer.

hints: First type: less manual.txt
Inside, type /OVERRIDE and press Enter; the view jumps to where that word appears.
Note the code, press q to quit, then submit it with answer.
1-12.title: Paging Through a Long File
1-12.story:
When a file is too long and you want to browse slowly, use less. It shows one page at a time, like flipping a book. Keys once you're inside:
  Space      next page
  b          previous page
  /keyword   search (type a slash, the word, then Enter)
  n          jump to the next match
  q          quit (important! otherwise you stay stuck inside)

The manual has 500 lines, and one section has been tampered with.
1-12.goal: Open the manual with less manual.txt, search for OVERRIDE, find that line, and submit its code with answer.
1-12.reveal: This section of the manual was altered. OVERRIDE is the only command code that can pause Warden, but the change was made the day before Vega vanished.

hints: Type man ls, then inside type /size and press Enter to search for the word size.
Find a line saying 'sort by file size'; the -X on its left is the option (X is an uppercase letter).
Press q to quit, then answer with that letter.
1-13.title: Read the Manual Yourself
1-13.story:
Nobody remembers every option of every command; experts just look things up faster. Linux has a built-in manual: man commandname (man = manual), e.g. man ls.

It works exactly like less: Space to page, /keyword to search, n for next, q to quit. The manual is in English, but each option like -S has a sentence next to it explaining what it does.
1-13.goal: Look up man ls, find the option letter that sorts by file size, and submit it with answer (just the letter, case matters, e.g. answer X).

hints: Type: which python3
The line it prints is the answer; paste it after answer.
1-14.title: Where Commands Live
1-14.story: Every command you type is really a program file on disk, which the system looks for in a fixed list of directories. which commandname tells you where that program actually lives (its full path). It's super useful for "I've installed several versions; which one am I actually running?"
1-14.goal: Use which python3 to find python3's full path and submit it with answer (the whole string starting with /).

hints: First type whoami, then hostname, and note the two outputs.
Join them with @ with no spaces.
1-15.title: Introduce Yourself
1-15.story:
When an admin takes over a machine, the first thing is to find out "who am I and which machine is this?"
  whoami    prints the user name you're logged in as
  hostname  prints this machine's name
Neither needs arguments; just type them alone.
1-15.goal: Run whoami and hostname, combine the results as user@host and submit, e.g. answer bob@server1.

hints: Type: uname -s (lowercase s).
Paste the word it prints after answer.
1-16.title: The System ID Card
1-16.story:
uname prints information about this computer's system (uname = Unix name). Different options ask different questions:
  uname -s   the operating system's name
  uname -r   the kernel version (the deepest core of the OS)
  uname -a   all of the above at once
Also, date prints the current date and time.
1-16.goal: Use uname -s to find the operating system name and submit it with answer.

hints: Type: echo Kernel-7 ready
The text must match exactly, including capitalization and the hyphen.
1-17.title: Talking to the Terminal
1-17.story:
echo prints whatever text you give it, exactly: echo hello prints "hello". Sounds silly, but it's one of the most-used commands in scripts and debugging (you'll use it a lot later).

Three handy tricks while we're here:
  clear or Ctrl-L   clear the screen
  history           see which commands you've typed
  Up arrow          recall the previous command so you needn't retype it
1-17.goal: Use echo to print the text Kernel-7 ready (echo, a space, then the text).

hints: First type: cat station/START.txt to read the first clue.
Follow the clue into the deck-3 directory, use ls to see what's there, then cat the note.txt inside.
Some files are hidden and need ls -a. This time the name is .vault; read it with cat .vault.
1-18.title: Boss: The Lost Password
1-18.story:
The final test! Vega hid the emergency password somewhere on the station, leaving a trail of clues, each pointing to the next. Use everything you've learned:
  pwd to see where you are, ls to see contents, ls -a to see hidden files
  cd to move, cat to read

It works like a treasure hunt: read a file → follow what it says → read the next one.
1-18.goal: Start at ~/station/START.txt, follow the clues to the hidden password, and submit it with answer.
1-18.reveal: The emergency password opened Vega's private channel. He left a message: "Go to the cargo bay on deck 2, the evidence is hidden there. Warden is always watching, so I can't say much." The message is timestamped 14:00, and the channel hasn't been updated since.

hints: The format is touch, a space, then the file name.
Type: touch notes.txt
Afterwards run ls; notes.txt should appear.
2-01.title: Create Your First File
2-01.story: A good cabin needs tidying. First, learn to make something from nothing: touch filename creates a new empty file (nothing inside). If the file already exists, its content is untouched; only its "last modified time" is set to now.
2-01.goal: In your current directory (your home), create an empty file named notes.txt.

hints: The format is mkdir, a space, then the directory name.
Type: mkdir cargo
Use ls to confirm cargo appeared.
2-02.title: Build a Cabin
2-02.story: mkdir means make directory, i.e. "create a folder": mkdir dirname. The station needs a dedicated place for cargo lists.

hints: Plain mkdir only makes one level; add -p to create the parents as well.
Format: mkdir -p PATH
Type: mkdir -p ship/deck/engine/core
2-03.title: Build a Whole Deck at Once
2-03.story:
To build several levels at once, say a containing b containing c, plain mkdir a/b/c fails because a and b don't exist yet.

Add the option -p (parents) and it "creates any missing parent directories too": mkdir -p a/b/c.
2-03.goal: With one command, create the four-level path ship/deck/engine/core.

hints: Format: cp sourcefile newname
Type: cp blueprint.txt blueprint.bak
Run ls; both files should be there.
2-04.title: Make a Backup
2-04.story:
Before editing something important, back it up first. cp (copy) works like this: cp source destination.

The original isn't touched; you just get an identical extra copy. If the destination is a new file name, you copy and give the copy that name.
2-04.goal: Copy blueprint.txt to blueprint.bak (keep the original).

hints: A bare cp config config-backup fails because config is a directory.
Add -r: cp -r sourcedir newdirname
Type: cp -r config config-backup
2-05.title: Back Up a Folder Too
2-05.story: By default cp only copies files and refuses directories. To copy a whole directory (with everything inside), add the option -r (recursive, meaning "do it level by level all the way down"): cp -r directory newname.
2-05.goal: Copy the whole config directory to config-backup.

hints: Format: mv oldname newname
Type: mv draft.txt final.txt
Run ls to confirm draft.txt is gone and final.txt appeared.
2-06.title: Rename
2-06.story:
Linux has no separate "rename" command. mv (move) handles both moving and renaming, because renaming is just "moving to a new name in the same place".

Format: mv oldname newname. Note that the old name disappears afterwards (unlike cp).

hints: The archive directory already exists; no need to create it.
Format: mv *.log archive/
Afterwards ls shows the .log files gone and readme.txt still there; ls archive shows what moved.
2-07.title: The Wildcard *
2-07.story:
Log files are scattered across your home, and moving them one by one is tedious. The asterisk * is a "wildcard" meaning "any number of any characters".

So *.log means "every file ending in .log". The shell expands it to the actual list of names before handing them to mv.

Format for moving into a directory: mv files targetdir/.
2-07.goal: Move all .log files into the archive directory (readme.txt isn't a .log, so it stays).
2-07.reveal: In the archived logs, there's a write every night at 03:00 that belongs to no one. The writer's name is warden.

hints: Format: rm filename
Type: rm junk.tmp (name only the one to delete)
Use ls to confirm junk.tmp is gone and keep.txt remains.
2-08.title: Taking Out the Trash
2-08.story:
rm (remove) deletes files: rm filename.

Be careful: Linux's rm has no recycle bin. Once deleted it's truly gone and can't be recovered, so look at the file name once more before pressing Enter.

hints: Use rm -r for directories with contents and rmdir for empty ones.
Type: rm -r old-station
Then type: rmdir empty
2-09.title: Demolish the Old Cabin
2-09.story:
There are two ways to delete a directory:
  rm -r dir    deletes it with everything inside (-r again means recursive; powerful, so be careful)
  rmdir dir    deletes only an empty directory and refuses otherwise, so it's safer

Tip for beginners: use rmdir whenever it works.
2-09.goal: Delete the old-station directory (it has contents) and the empty directory empty. Keep the keep directory.

hints: The question mark ? stands for one character, so report-?.txt only matches single-digit names.
Preview with ls report-?.txt first to check what it matches.
If it looks right, type: rm report-?.txt
2-10.title: Wildcards ? and []
2-10.story:
Besides *, there are more precise wildcards:
  ?       stands for exactly ONE of any character. report-?.txt matches report-1.txt but not report-10.txt (two characters there).
  [abc]   stands for any ONE character listed inside the brackets. report-[12].txt matches report-1.txt and report-2.txt.

With them you can pick a precise group of files.
2-10.goal: Delete report-1.txt through report-9.txt (single digit), but keep report-10.txt and report-final.txt.

hints: Separate items inside the braces with commas, no spaces next to them.
touch can create several files at once; follow it with the brace expression.
Type: touch log-{jan,feb,mar}.txt
2-11.title: Brace Expansion
2-11.story:
Curly braces {a,b,c} are a shell "expansion" feature: one expression becomes several.

For example log-{jan,feb,mar}.txt automatically turns into three words: log-jan.txt log-feb.txt log-mar.txt. So one command can create three files at once (no spaces after the commas).
2-11.goal: Using brace expansion, create log-jan.txt, log-feb.txt and log-mar.txt with one command.

hints: Wrap the whole file name in double quotes "".
Type: touch "my notes.txt"
You can also put a backslash before the space: touch my\ notes.txt
2-12.title: Quotes and Spaces
2-12.story:
The shell uses spaces to split a command line into words. So if a file name contains a space, like my notes.txt, the shell thinks you mean two files: my and notes.txt.

The fix is to wrap the whole name in quotes so it counts as one piece: touch "my notes.txt".
2-12.goal: Create a file named my notes.txt (with a space in the middle).

hints: Format: ln -s target linkname; the target comes first, the new name second.
Type: ln -s logs/2024-05.log latest.log
ls -l shows latest.log -> logs/2024-05.log.
2-13.title: Symbolic Links (Shortcuts)
2-13.story:
A "symbolic link" (symlink) is like a Windows shortcut: it's a tiny file whose content is just "the path to another file". Opening it is like opening the target.

Format: ln -s target linkname (-s means symbolic). Typical use: make latest.log always point at the newest log, changing only where it points.
2-13.goal: Create a symlink latest.log that points to logs/2024-05.log.
2-13.reveal: The shortcut latest.log has been repointed. Someone (or something) is secretly altering your paths.

hints: Use ln like for symlinks, but without -s.
Format: ln original newname
Type: ln data.txt data-link.txt, then ls -li shows both with the same inode number at the start.
2-14.title: Hard Links
2-14.story:
A "hard link" is a second name for the same data. File data on disk has a number (an inode); a hard link makes two names point to the same number.

So deleting one name leaves the data intact, since the other name still holds it. The syntax is like a symlink without -s: ln original newname.
2-14.goal: Create a hard link data-link.txt for data.txt.

hints: Format: file filename
Type: file mystery
The format name appears in the output; answer it in lowercase.
2-15.title: Detective: file and stat
2-15.story:
A file extension (like .txt) is just part of the name and can be changed at will, so it isn't always trustworthy. To learn what a file really is, use file filename: it peeks at the contents to decide the type.
(There's also stat filename for more detail such as size and times.)
2-15.goal: The file mystery has no extension. Use file mystery to find which compression format it is and submit it with answer (one of gzip, bzip2 or zip).

hints: First cd storage.
Type: du -sh *; each item shows its size.
Compare sizes (K < M < G); the biggest directory's name is the answer.
2-16.title: Who's Taking the Space
2-16.story:
The disk is nearly full! To find who's hogging space:
  du -sh dir   total size of a directory (du = disk usage; -s gives only the total, -h uses readable units like MB and GB)
  df -h        how much free space each disk has

In du -sh *, the * expands to every item here, so you see each one's size at once.
2-16.goal: Find which sub-directory under storage is the biggest and submit its name with answer.

hints: Type: tree vault
The file indented the furthest to the right is the deepest.
Answer its full file name, including the extension after the dot.
2-17.title: See the Whole Tree
2-17.story:
tree draws a directory structure as a tree so you can see at a glance what's inside what:
  tree dir    draw the whole tree
  tree -L 2   show only two levels deep (-L limits depth)
  tree -a     include hidden files too
2-17.goal: Use tree vault to inspect this directory, find the file at the deepest level (with extension) and submit it with answer.

hints: First cd downloads, then create all three at once: mkdir images docs music
mv can move several patterns at once: mv *.jpg *.png images/
Likewise: mv *.pdf *.txt docs/ and mv *.mp3 music/. Finally ls to check only the .zip remains.
2-18.title: Boss: Tidy the Downloads
2-18.story:
The downloads folder is a disaster zone! Use your mkdir, mv and wildcard skills to sort by type:
  images (.jpg .png) → images
  documents (.pdf .txt) → docs
  music (.mp3) → music
Leave the .zip file alone for now.
2-18.goal: In downloads, create the directories images, docs and music; move .jpg/.png into images, .pdf/.txt into docs, .mp3 into music. Leave the .zip file where it is.
2-18.reveal: After tidying the downloads, you notice a backup.zip nobody downloaded, and inside it is warden-installer. Warden isn't factory equipment: someone installed it on the station. The installer field has been wiped blank.

hints: Format: find where-to-look -name filename
Type: find ship -name radar.cfg
It prints one path; answer that whole line.
3-01.title: find: Search by Name
3-01.story:
The station has thousands of files; you can't browse them one by one. find starts at a directory you give it and searches level after level until it finds things matching your condition.

The most basic condition is the name: find startdir -name filename
Meaning: "starting here, find files with this name", and it prints each match's full location.
3-01.goal: Find where radar.cfg is under the ship directory and submit the path it prints with answer.

hints: Swap -name for -iname: find docs -iname readme
To count, add | wc -l and you get a number.
Type: find docs -iname readme | wc -l, then answer that number.
3-02.title: Ignoring Case
3-02.story:
Linux is case sensitive: README, Readme and readme are three different files. If you're not sure of the case, swap -name for -iname (i = ignore), which disregards case.

To count results, add | wc -l (the | hands the output on to the next command; wc -l counts lines, and each result is one line, so the line count is the number of results).
3-02.goal: Under docs, find all files named readme (any case, no extension) and submit how many there are with answer.

hints: Write both conditions: -type d (directories only) plus -name backup.
Type: find archive -type d -name backup
Count the lines printed (or add | wc -l) and answer that number.
3-03.title: Find by Type
3-03.story:
find can also filter by type, using -type:
  -type f   only files
  -type d   only directories
  -type l   only symbolic links
You can combine it with -name; an item must satisfy both conditions to be listed.
3-03.goal: Under archive, how many directories are named backup? Submit the count with answer (files named backup don't count).

hints: For "bigger than", put + before the number.
Type: find cargo -size +1M
Answer the file name at the end of the path it prints.
3-04.title: Find by Size
3-04.story:
-size filters by file size:
  -size +1M   bigger than 1 MB (+ means "more than")
  -size -10k  smaller than 10 KB (- means "less than")
The units are k for KB, M for MB and G for GB. Great for cleaning disks and hunting fat files.
3-04.goal: Under cargo, find the file larger than 1MB and submit its file name with answer.

hints: Preview first (no deleting): find tmp -type f -mtime +30 and check the list is what you want to delete.
If the list is right, add -delete at the end of the same line.
Type: find tmp -type f -mtime +30 -delete
3-05.title: Find by Time, and Delete
3-05.story:
-mtime filters by "how many days ago it was last modified":
  -mtime +30   modified more than 30 days ago (old files)
  -mtime -3    modified within 3 days (new files)
Add -delete and the matches are removed directly, a handy way to auto-clean stale files.

Warning: -delete must come last and deletion is permanent. Beginners: preview the list without -delete first, then add it once the list is right.
3-05.goal: Delete the files under tmp that haven't been modified in over 30 days; keep the recent ones.

hints: First run find scripts -name '*.sh' to see which files match (wrap '*.sh' in single quotes).
Then append: -exec chmod +x {} \;
Full command: find scripts -name '*.sh' -exec chmod +x {} \;
3-06.title: find with -exec
3-06.story:
-exec makes find run a command on "each result it finds". The shape is:
  find start conditions -exec command {} \;
Here {} is replaced by each found file name, and \; marks the end of the command (the backslash keeps the shell from misreading the semicolon).

For example -exec chmod +x {} \; runs chmod +x on each found file (chmod +x means "make the file executable"; stage 5 covers it in detail).
3-06.goal: None of the .sh files under scripts are executable. Use find with -exec chmod +x to fix them all at once.

hints: Format: grep keyword filename
Type: grep FATAL app.log
Find the code starting with E at the end of the printed line and answer it.
3-07.title: grep: Search Contents
3-07.story:
find searches for file names; grep searches for text inside files.

grep keyword filename prints every line of the file that contains the keyword, whole line. It's like highlighting, in a very thick book, every sentence with a certain word.
3-07.goal: Only one line in app.log contains FATAL. Find it with grep and submit the error code at its end (the string starting with E) via answer.

hints: Format: grep -in keyword filename
Type: grep -in password server.conf
The number before the colon at the start of the output is the line number; answer it.
3-08.title: grep -i -n
3-08.story:
Two commonly used grep options:
  -i   ignore case (Password, PASSWORD and password all count)
  -n   print the line number in front of each line
They can be combined as -in. When managing config files you often need to know which line a setting is on.
3-08.goal: server.conf has a line containing password (case unknown). Use grep -in to find its line number and submit it with answer.

hints: Format: grep -r keyword directory
Type: grep -r api_key= project
Output looks like "filename:content"; answer the value after api_key=.
3-09.title: grep -r Recursive Search
3-09.story:
A project has hundreds or thousands of files; you can't grep them one by one. Add -r (recursive) and grep searches all files under a whole directory: grep -r keyword directory. Each output line is prefixed with the file it came from.

Someone hard-coded an API key (a password a program uses to access a service) in a project file. Find it.
3-09.goal: Search for api_key= under the project directory and submit the value after = with answer.
3-09.reveal: The key k3y-8812-zz appears in prod.env, where it doesn't belong. Something is copying secrets around.

hints: First see what remains: grep -v '^#' app.conf (-v excludes lines starting with #).
To get just the number, add -c.
Type: grep -vc '^#' app.conf and answer that number.
3-10.title: grep -v and -c
3-10.story:
Two very handy options:
  -v   invert: print lines that do NOT contain the keyword
  -c   don't print the content, just tell how many lines matched (c = count)

In config files, lines starting with # are comments (notes for humans that have no effect). '^#' is a tiny pattern meaning "starts with #" (^ means the start of a line). So grep -v '^#' means "exclude comments".
3-10.goal: Lines in app.conf that start with # are comments. Count the non-comment lines and submit with answer.

hints: Use -r to search a whole directory and -l for names only, so the options together are -rl.
Simple version: grep -rl '192.168' leak
Advanced version (regex): grep -rlE '192\.168\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' leak, then answer the printed name (b.txt).
3-11.title: grep -l and -E
3-11.story:
This level introduces two new things:

① -l (lowercase L): don't print the matching content, only the names of files that contain a match. With -r it means "which files contain this word".

② A "regular expression": a way of describing the shape of text. You want to find an IP address but don't know exactly what it is, only that it starts with 192.168. and has two more groups of digits.
   A . here means "any one character"; to match a real dot write \.
   [0-9] means "one digit", and a + after it means "one or more"
   So 192\.168\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+ means "192.168. followed by two groups of digits". For this style add -E and wrap it in single quotes.

(Lazy version: just searching for the start, grep -rl '192.168' leak, also passes here.)
3-11.goal: In the leak directory, find the file containing an IP address starting with 192.168. and submit the file name with answer.

hints: To see the line after the match, use -A 1.
Type: grep -A 1 CRITICAL reactor.log
Find cause= on the second output line and answer the value after it.
3-12.title: Context: -A -B -C
3-12.story:
Seeing only the error line is often not enough; the cause is usually written near it. grep can print the surrounding lines too:
  -A NUMBER   After: also print that many lines after the match
  -B NUMBER   Before: also print that many lines before
  -C NUMBER   Context: both before and after
For example grep -A 1 CRITICAL file finds the CRITICAL line and also prints the line right after it.
3-12.goal: reactor.log has a line with CRITICAL, and the line after it says cause=SOME REASON. Use grep -A to find it and submit the value after cause= with answer.
3-12.reveal: The reactor overheated because of a coolant leak. But one minute before the leak, someone issued a command that lowered the flow.

hints: First run find work -name '*.bak' alone and check those are the files to delete.
Append: | xargs rm
Full command: find work -name '*.bak' | xargs rm
3-13.title: xargs: Handing Results to Others
3-13.story:
The pipe | feeds one command's output into the next command as input. But some commands (like rm) don't read input; they only look at the file names you write after them.

xargs is the translator: it turns what it receives into file-name arguments for the next command. So:
  find work -name '*.bak' | xargs rm
means "find all .bak files, then hand them all to rm to delete".
3-13.goal: Delete all .bak files under work and keep everything else. Use find with xargs.

hints: Format: locate filename
Type: locate starmap.dat
Answer the whole path it prints.
3-14.title: locate: Fast System-Wide Search
3-14.story:
find has to really walk the directories each time, which is slow over a large area. locate instead uses a pre-built "index" of all file names on the system, so lookups are nearly instant: locate filename.

The downside is the index must be refreshed periodically (with updatedb), so very new files may not be found yet.
3-14.goal: The star chart file starmap.dat is hidden somewhere on the system. Use locate to find its full path and submit it with answer.

hints: First type: grep -r 'sk_live_' webapp to see which file and what content.
The output looks like "filename:content"; answer the complete sk_live_… key.
Then use rm to delete that file from the output (only the one with sk_live_; leave sk_test_ ones alone).
3-15.title: Boss: The Leaked Key
3-15.story:
Emergency! Someone committed a "production key" (a string starting with sk_live_, a password that can really affect the live service) into the project. You must find it, report it, and delete the file that contains it.

Use this stage's skills: grep -r to search contents, -l for file names only, rm to delete.
Note: strings starting with sk_test_ are test keys; they're fine, don't delete those by mistake.
3-15.goal: In the webapp project, find the key starting with sk_live_ (submit the full key with answer) and delete the file containing it.
3-15.reveal: You deleted the leaked key, and Warden's outside connection went down for a full hour. But Pip noticed something odd: the key wasn't stolen, Warden released it itself, like a call for help. What you cut off may not have been an attack, but a cry for help.

hints: One member per line, so the line count is the head count.
Format: wc -l filename
Type: wc -l crew.txt; the number at the start of the output is the answer.
4-01.title: wc: Count Things
4-01.story:
Now into the soul of Unix: text processing. Linux stores settings, logs and data almost entirely as plain text, so handling text means controlling the whole system.

First tool, wc (word count):
  wc -l file   count lines (l = lines)
  wc -w file   count words
  wc -c file   count bytes
4-01.goal: crew.txt has one crew member per line. Use wc -l to count the crew and submit with answer.

hints: Format: echo text > filename
Type: echo mission-start > log.txt
Check with cat log.txt; you should see mission-start.
4-02.title: Redirect >
4-02.story:
Normally a command's result is printed on screen. The "redirect" symbol > sends it into a file instead:
  command > filename
For example echo hello > a.txt shows nothing on screen but writes hello into a.txt.
Note: > overwrites the file's previous content; if the file doesn't exist it's created.
4-02.goal: Using echo with >, write the text mission-start into log.txt.

hints: It's two greater-than signs >>, not one.
Format: echo text >> filename
Type: echo Pip >> roster.txt, then cat roster.txt should show three lines.
4-03.title: Append >>
4-03.story:
The > from the last level wipes the whole file. To add to the end without destroying the old content, use two greater-than signs >> (append):
  echo new line >> filename
When writing logs always use >>, or all the old records vanish.
4-03.goal: roster.txt already has two members. Append a line Pip with >>, keeping the original two lines intact.

hints: | is the vertical bar, usually above the Enter key (hold Shift).
Type: ls hangar | wc -l
The number printed is the answer.
4-04.title: The Pipe |
4-04.story:
The pipe symbol | (the vertical bar key, usually above Enter) hands the output of the previous command to the next one as input, like connecting pipes:
  commandA | commandB
Each tool does one thing, and chained together they handle complex jobs.

For example ls hangar prints many file names (one per line), and adding | wc -l counts the lines, telling you how many files there are.
4-04.goal: The hangar directory has many files. Use ls hangar | wc -l to count them and submit with answer.

hints: First sort, so duplicates end up next to each other.
Then | uniq removes them, and > saves to a file.
Type: sort names.txt | uniq > unique.txt (or sort -u names.txt > unique.txt)
4-05.title: sort and uniq: Removing Duplicates
4-05.story:
uniq removes duplicate lines, but only ADJACENT duplicates; it can't see ones that are apart. So first use sort to bring identical lines together, then uniq:
  sort file | uniq
Join them with a pipe, and finish with > to save into a file.
(Another way: sort -u does the sorting and de-duplicating in one step.)
4-05.goal: names.txt has duplicate names. Sort and de-duplicate it, saving the result as unique.txt.

hints: First sort -nr scores.txt orders all scores biggest to smallest.
Then pipe into head -3 to keep only the first 3 lines.
Type: sort -nr scores.txt | head -3 > top3.txt
4-06.title: Numeric Sort
4-06.story:
sort orders "alphabetically" by default: comparing 100 with 20, the character 1 comes before 2, so 100 is placed before 20, which isn't what we want.

  sort -n   sort by numeric value (n = numeric)
  sort -r   reverse, biggest first (r = reverse)
They combine as -nr. Then head -3 takes the first 3 lines, i.e. the "top three".
4-06.goal: scores.txt has one score per line. Find the top three and save them to top3.txt (largest first).

hints: First sort ips.txt so equal IPs are adjacent, then | uniq -c to count.
Then | sort -nr orders most-first, and | head -1 takes the top.
Type: sort ips.txt | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -1, and answer the IP in the output (not the count in front).
4-07.title: The Leaderboard: uniq -c
4-07.story:
The classic text-analysis trio, worth memorising:
  sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
Steps: ① sort brings identical lines together ② uniq -c merges duplicates into one line and prints "how many times" in front (c = count) ③ sort -nr orders by count, most first.
The result is a "leaderboard"; add head -1 for the winner.
4-07.goal: ips.txt is a visitor IP record (one per line). Find the IP that appears most often and submit it with answer.
4-07.reveal: The most frequent visitor IP is 10.0.0.9. It doesn't belong to any crew member's device.

hints: The score is column 3, so use -k3; fields are comma-separated, so use -t,
To compare numbers biggest-first, add -nr.
Type: sort -t, -k3 -nr crew.csv | head -1, and answer the name at the start of that line.
4-08.title: Sort by Column
4-08.story:
CSV is a common table format: one record per line, fields separated by commas, e.g.:
  Alice,pilot,92
To sort such data you must tell sort two things:
  -t,    the field separator is a comma (t = field separator)
  -k3    sort by the 3rd column (k = key)
Add -nr to order scores biggest first.
4-08.goal: Each line of crew.csv is name,role,score. Find the person with the highest score and submit their name with answer.

hints: Email is column 2, and fields are comma-separated.
Format: cut -dSEPARATOR -fNUMBER filename
Type: cut -d, -f2 users.csv > emails.txt
4-09.title: cut: Slicing Out Columns
4-09.story:
cut is like a paper cutter that slices out the column you want from each line:
  -d,   tells it fields are separated by commas (d = delimiter)
  -f2   take the 2nd field (f = field)
For a line Bob,bob@mail.com,ops, cut -d, -f2 gives bob@mail.com.
4-09.goal: Each line of users.csv is name,email,department. Extract column 2 (the email) and save it as emails.txt.

hints: tr can't take a file name; use < to feed the file in.
Format: tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' < inputfile > outputfile
Type: tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' < msg.txt > loud.txt
4-10.title: tr: Character Translation
4-10.story:
tr (translate) swaps characters one by one: tr 'old chars' 'new chars' replaces each character of the first set with the one in the same position of the second.
  a-z means "lowercase a through z" and A-Z the uppercase, so tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' means "lowercase to uppercase".

tr is special: it doesn't take a file name, it only reads input. So feed it a file with <:
  tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' < inputfile > outputfile
4-10.goal: Convert all lowercase letters in msg.txt to uppercase and save the result as loud.txt.

hints: Use -d to delete; the character to delete is \r (remember the quotes).
Format: tr -d '\r' < inputfile > outputfile
Type: tr -d '\r' < dos.txt > clean.txt
4-11.title: Cleaning Windows Line Endings
4-11.story:
Text files from Windows have an invisible character CR (written \r) at the end of each line, which causes odd errors on Linux.

tr can also delete characters: tr -d chars (d = delete). So tr -d '\r' removes every \r. Again feed the file with < and save with >.
4-11.goal: dos.txt contains CR characters. Delete them all and save the result as clean.txt.

hints: Normal results use >, errors use 2>, each followed by a file name.
Format: command > found.txt 2> errors.txt
Type: find /root /etc -name '*.conf' > found.txt 2> errors.txt
4-12.title: Error Output 2>
4-12.story:
A program actually has two output "pipes":
  #1: normal output (results)
  #2: error output (error messages)
Both print on screen by default. The > you've learned only catches #1; to save errors separately use 2>.
  command > resultfile 2> errorfile
(find prints errors when it hits directories you have no permission for, which is perfect practice.)
4-12.goal: Run find /root /etc -name '*.conf': save the normal results into found.txt and the error messages into errors.txt.

hints: First enter cat > motd.txt << EOF and press Enter; the cursor waits for more input.
Then type each line: Welcome, aboard, Kernel-7, pressing Enter after each.
Finally type EOF alone on a line and press Enter. Check with cat motd.txt.
4-13.title: Here Document
4-13.story:
How do you type several lines of text straight into a file from the terminal? Use a Here Document:
  cat > filename << EOF
  (then type the content line by line)
  EOF
Meaning: "treat everything I type from now on as the file's content, until I type a line with just EOF". EOF (End Of File) is only an agreed signal word and can be any word. Super handy for config files and scripts.
4-13.goal: Use cat > motd.txt << EOF to create a three-line file containing Welcome, aboard, Kernel-7 in order, ending with a line of just EOF.

hints: First ls /etc | head -5 takes the first 5 lines.
Then add | tee first5.txt; the result is shown and saved.
Type: ls /etc | head -5 | tee first5.txt
4-14.title: tee: Watch and Save
4-14.story:
tee is like a T-junction in a pipe: data keeps flowing onward (printed on screen) while a copy is saved into a file. Saving with > hides the output from the screen, but tee lets you "watch and save":
  command | tee filename
4-14.goal: Take the first 5 lines of ls /etc and use tee to show them on screen and save them as first5.txt at the same time.

hints: To edit the file directly, use -i.
Format: sed -i 's/old/new/g' filename
Type: sed -i 's/localhost/10.0.0.5/g' app.conf, then cat app.conf to check.
4-15.title: sed: Search and Replace
4-15.story:
sed is a "stream editor", like a word processor's Find & Replace but driven by commands. The most common form:
  sed 's/old/new/g' filename
Meaning: replace "old" with "new" on every line (s = substitute; g = global, replace all occurrences on a line).
Normally sed just prints the result and the file doesn't change; add -i (in-place) to really rewrite the file. Think about a backup before editing.
4-15.goal: Replace every localhost in app.conf with 10.0.0.5, editing the file itself.

hints: Format: sed -n 'FROM,TOp' filename
FROM is 10 and TO is 12.
Type: sed -n '10,12p' story.txt > mid.txt
4-16.title: sed: Extract Specific Lines
4-16.story:
sed can also pick out specific lines:
  sed -n '10,12p' filename
Here -n is "quiet mode" (don't print every line by default); '10,12p' means "lines 10 through 12", with p for print. So only those three lines are printed.
4-16.goal: story.txt has 30 lines. Extract lines 10 to 12 and save them as mid.txt.

hints: One at a time: sed -i '/^#/d' config.ini removes comments first.
Then handle blank lines with the rule /^$/d.
Both together: sed -i '/^#/d;/^$/d' config.ini
4-17.title: sed: Delete Lines
4-17.story:
sed can also delete whole lines: sed '/pattern/d' filename means "delete every line matching this pattern" (d = delete).
  '/^#/d'   delete lines starting with # (^ means line start, i.e. comments)
  '/^$/d'   delete empty lines (^$ means "line start immediately followed by line end", nothing between)
To give two rules at once, separate them with a semicolon. Add -i to really modify the file.
4-17.goal: config.ini is full of comments (starting with #) and blank lines. Edit the file in place, deleting all comments and blank lines so only the settings remain.

hints: The amount is the 3rd field, so use $3.
Format: awk '{s+=$3} END{print s}' filename
Type: awk '{s+=$3} END{print s}' sales.txt, and answer the number printed.
4-18.title: awk: Calculate by Column
4-18.story:
awk is great at data with one record per line and several columns per line. It automatically splits each line on whitespace into fields: the 1st is $1, the 2nd $2, and so on.

  awk '{s+=$3} END{print s}' filename
Meaning: for each line read, add the 3rd field to variable s (s+=$3); after everything is read (END), print s. That gives the total.
4-18.goal: Each line of sales.txt is "item quantity amount". Compute the sum of the amount (3rd field) and submit with answer.

hints: CSV is comma-separated, so use -F,
The condition is $3>80 and the action is printing field 1: {print $1}.
Type: awk -F, '$3>80{print $1}' crew.csv > elite.txt
4-19.title: awk: Filter by Condition
4-19.story:
awk lets you put a "condition" before the action so only matching lines run it:
  awk 'condition{action}' filename
  -F,   fields are comma-separated (default is whitespace)
  $3>80   the 3rd field is greater than 80
  print $1   print the 1st field
So awk -F, '$3>80{print $1}' means "for people scoring over 80, print the name".
4-19.goal: Each line of crew.csv is name,role,score. Save the names of people with a score above 80 to elite.txt (one per line).

hints: Format: diff oldfile newfile
Type: diff old.conf new.conf
Find the line starting with > (it belongs to new.conf) and answer the value after port=.
4-20.title: diff: Finding Differences
4-20.story:
diff compares two files and shows where they differ:
  diff oldfile newfile
In the output, lines starting with < come from the first file and lines starting with > from the second. Great for "I changed a setting; what exactly changed?" (Adding -u gives a more readable git-style format.)
4-20.goal: old.conf and new.conf differ on just one line. Find it with diff and submit the value of port= in the new file (new.conf) with answer.
4-20.reveal: The old and new config files differ by just one port, changed to 9090, exactly the port Warden has been secretly listening on.

hints: First look at the data: jq '.crew[]' crew.json
To filter pilots use select(.role=="pilot"), then take .name.
Type: jq -r '.crew[] | select(.role=="pilot") | .name' crew.json
4-21.title: jq: Handling JSON
4-21.story:
Modern web services mostly return data in JSON, which looks like:
  {"crew": [{"name": "Ann", "role": "pilot"}, ...]}
grep struggles with it. jq is a tool built for JSON:
  .crew         pick out the crew field
  .crew[]       take each item of the list one by one
  select(cond)  keep only items matching the condition
  -r            output plain text without quotes
4-21.goal: crew.json is the crew list. Find the person whose role is pilot and submit their name with answer.

hints: Format: paste file1 file2
Save the result into a file with >.
Type: paste names.txt ages.txt > people.tsv
4-22.title: paste and Other Small Tools
4-22.story:
paste glues files together side by side: line 1 of the first file is joined to line 1 of the second, and so on (separated by a Tab), like pasting two columns of data into one table.

A few other small tools: nl adds line numbers, column -t aligns data into a table, rev reverses each line, and fold wraps long lines.
4-22.goal: Merge names.txt and ages.txt side by side with paste and save as people.tsv.

hints: First pull out all emails: grep -oE '[A-Za-z0-9._]+@[A-Za-z0-9.]+' contacts.txt
Remove duplicates by adding | sort -u (sort and de-duplicate).
Then add | wc -l to count lines. Full: grep -oE '[A-Za-z0-9._]+@[A-Za-z0-9.]+' contacts.txt | sort -u | wc -l
4-23.title: Regular Expressions
4-23.story:
A "regular expression" is shorthand for describing the shape of text, letting you find strings that look like a certain format, such as an email. Basic building blocks:
  [A-Za-z0-9._]   one character that may be a letter, digit, dot or underscore
  +               the previous piece repeated one or more times
  @               just the @ itself
So [A-Za-z0-9._]+@[A-Za-z0-9.]+ means "a run of characters, an @, then another run", which is the shape of an email.

grep -oE 'shape' file: -E enables this syntax, and -o prints only the matching piece rather than the whole line.
4-23.goal: contacts.txt is a messy text with emails scattered through it. Find how many distinct emails there are and submit the count with answer.

hints: Each log line looks like: IP - - [date:hour:min:sec +0000] "GET path HTTP/1.1" status size. The IP is field 1, the time field 4, the status field 9.
Most frequent IP: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -1
Busiest hour: awk '{print $4}' access.log | cut -d: -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -1 (split field 4 on colons; the 2nd piece is the hour)
Total 5xx: awk '$9 ~ /^5/' access.log | wc -l ($9 ~ /^5/ means field 9 starts with 5)
Combine the three results into one answer, e.g. answer 10.0.0.1 12 09
4-24.title: Boss: Server Log Analysis
4-24.story:
The website is being slammed! The boss wants three numbers: the most frequent IP, the total number of 5xx errors, and the busiest hour. (5xx means status codes 500-599, i.e. server-side errors.)

This needs everything from the stage chained together: awk to pick fields, cut to slice strings, sort | uniq -c | sort -nr for leaderboards, wc -l to count.
Go step by step: check each stage's output before adding the next pipe.
4-24.goal: Analyze access.log and submit three values separated by spaces with answer: the most frequent IP, the total number of requests with 5xx status, and the hour with the most requests (two digits, e.g. 14). Example: answer 10.0.0.1 12 09
4-24.reveal: Traffic peaks cluster at 14:00, the exact moment Vega vanished. Stranger still, the source of the spike isn't an outside intrusion but the station itself: something filled the disk all at once at 14:00.

hints: Just type id, nothing else.
Find the number after uid= and before the parenthesis.
To print only the uid, type id -u.
5-01.title: Who Am I
5-01.story:
Linux is a multi-user system. Every user (account) has a numeric ID called a uid (user id), and every group has a gid. The system really uses these numbers to tell "who is who".

The id command shows your identity, with output like:
  uid=1000(player) gid=1000(player) groups=1000(player)
The number outside the parentheses is the ID; the name is inside.
5-01.goal: Use id to find your user number (uid) and submit that number with answer.

hints: Type ls -l and look at each file's permission string on the left.
Only look at the last three characters; those are others' permissions.
The file whose last three characters include a w (like rw-) is the answer.
5-02.title: Reading Permission Strings
5-02.story:
The string at the far left of each ls -l line, like -rw-r--r--, is the file's "permissions", 10 characters:
  1st: the type (- for a file, d for a directory)
  then three groups of three characters for "owner | group | others"
  each group's characters are r (read), w (write), x (execute), or - if absent
So -rw-r--r-- means: the owner can read and write, the group can only read, and others can only read.

One file was accidentally made "writable by anyone", which is dangerous.
5-02.goal: One of a.txt, b.txt and c.txt can be written by "others" too (a w in the last three characters). Find it and submit the file name with answer.

hints: Owner is u, add is +, execute is x.
Format: chmod u+x filename
Type: chmod u+x script.sh, then ls -l shows an extra x in the first group.
5-03.title: chmod: Make a Script Executable
5-03.story:
Newly created files can't be executed by default (no x); a script needs "execute permission" added before it can run. chmod (change mode) changes permissions:
  chmod who action permission filename
who: u (owner), g (group), o (others), a (everyone)
action: + add, - remove
permission: r read, w write, x execute
For example chmod u+x filename = "owner, add, execute".
5-03.goal: script.sh has no execute permission. Use chmod to let the owner (you) run it.

hints: The owner needs rw = 4+2 = 6; group and others need 0.
Format: chmod number filename
Type: chmod 600 secret.txt
5-04.title: Octal Permissions
5-04.story:
Besides writing rwx, permissions can be written as numbers:
  r = 4   w = 2   x = 1
Add up what each group has: rwx = 4+2+1 = 7; rw- = 4+2 = 6; r-- = 4; --- = 0.
The three groups (owner, group, others) become three digits in a row:
  755 = rwxr-xr-x
  644 = rw-r--r--
  600 = rw------- (only the owner can read and write)
5-04.goal: secret.txt is confidential. Make it readable and writable only by the owner, with no permissions at all for anyone else (600).

hints: First try cd vault to see the error, then ls -ld vault to see the permissions (-d looks at the directory itself).
The owner needs r and x, so add x: chmod u+x vault
Or use numbers: chmod 700 vault (owner gets everything).
5-05.title: What x Means on a Directory
5-05.story:
Permissions mean something slightly different on directories:
  r: you can list what's inside (ls)
  x: you can "enter" the directory (cd) and reach things inside
Without x, even with r, cd is refused (Permission denied).
5-05.goal: The vault directory's permissions are wrong and even you can't enter it. Fix it so the owner can enter and list its contents.

hints: a is everyone, +r adds read, and capital X means "execute only for directories".
It's for the whole tree, so add -R.
Type: chmod -R a+rX public
5-06.title: Recursion and Capital X
5-06.story:
To apply permissions to a whole directory tree (a directory and everything inside), use -R (recursive): chmod -R.

But there's a trap: directories need x to be entered, while ordinary files shouldn't have x. Use a capital X for that: it adds x only to directories (and files already executable), so plain files don't accidentally become executable.
  chmod -R a+rX dir   everyone can read, and directories can be entered
5-06.goal: Make the public tree world read-only: every file readable by others, every directory readable and enterable by others. Files must not gain execute permission.

hints: What changes is "others" (o): remove read and write.
Type: chmod o-rw shared.txt
Or use numbers directly: chmod 660 shared.txt
5-07.title: Adjusting Several Groups at Once
5-07.story:
Symbolic mode lets you list several adjustments separated by commas:
  g+w,o-rwx   add write for the group and remove all of others' permissions (r, w and x)
You can also touch just one group and permission, e.g. o-rw means "others, remove read and write".
5-07.goal: shared.txt is currently readable and writable by everyone (666). Change it so the owner and group can read and write, and others have no permissions at all (660).

hints: First type cat /root/mission.txt and you'll see Permission denied.
Put sudo in front of the same command: sudo cat /root/mission.txt
Find the code after MISSION: and answer it.
5-08.title: sudo: Borrowing root's Power
5-08.story:
root is the system's super administrator: it can do anything, including accidentally breaking the whole system, so you shouldn't normally log in as root.

For admin work, put sudo (superuser do) before a command to "run just this one command as root"; afterwards you're an ordinary user again.
  sudo command
5-08.goal: /root/mission.txt can only be read by root. Read it with sudo cat and submit the code after MISSION: with answer.
5-08.reveal: Warden's permission notes contain a project code name: AURORA-5. The whole content is blacked out, leaving only one line: "Authorization level: unlimited." No wonder it can change any file.

hints: Format: sudo chown owner:group file
Both owner and group must be player, so write player:player.
Type: sudo chown player:player /srv/engine/engine.log, then confirm with ls -l.
5-09.title: chown: Changing the Owner
5-09.story:
Every file has an "owner" and a "group". A file created by root can't be changed by you. chown (change owner) changes the owner, in the format:
  chown owner:group file
(left of the colon is the new owner, right is the new group.) It needs root power, so put sudo in front.
5-09.goal: /srv/engine/engine.log belongs to root and you can't write to it. Use sudo chown to make both its owner and group player.

hints: Format: sudo useradd -m username
-m creates the home directory; don't forget it.
Type: sudo useradd -m cadet, then ls /home should show cadet.
5-10.title: Adding a User
5-10.story:
A new crew member has arrived! useradd creates a user account:
  sudo useradd -m username
The -m means "also create their home directory" (/home/username); without it the account has no folder of its own. Managing users needs root power, so add sudo.
5-10.goal: Create a user called cadet and make sure they have a home directory /home/cadet.

hints: First create the group: sudo groupadd engineers
Then add the user: sudo usermod -aG engineers cadet
Check with id cadet or groups cadet; you should see engineers.
5-11.title: Group Management
5-11.story:
A "group" is a set of users. Granting permissions to a group is like granting them to everyone in it at once, with no need to do it one by one.
  sudo groupadd groupname              create a group
  sudo usermod -aG groupname user      add a user to a group
Important: in usermod's -aG the a (append) must never be left out, or the user is removed from all their other groups.
5-11.goal: Create the group engineers and add the user cadet to it.

hints: Type: getent passwd quartermaster
The output has seven colon-separated fields; the last is the login shell.
Answer the content of that field (a path starting with /).
5-12.title: The Account Database
5-12.story:
All users' data lives in the text file /etc/passwd, one account per line, split by colons into seven fields:
  name:password:uid:gid:comment:home:login-shell
The standard way to look up one account is getent passwd name. The "login shell" is the shell program they get after logging in (the last field, e.g. /bin/bash).
5-12.goal: Find the login shell of the user quartermaster and submit it with answer (e.g. /bin/xxx).

hints: First try cat /home/ghost/note.txt; it will be refused.
Format: sudo -u user command
Type: sudo -u ghost cat /home/ghost/note.txt and answer the code word.
5-13.title: Running as Someone Else
5-13.story:
Sometimes you want to know "what a certain user can actually see". sudo -u user command runs a single command "as that user" (-u = user).

ghost's home directory can only be entered by ghost, so reading directly is refused, but borrowing his identity works.
5-13.goal: Use sudo -u ghost to read /home/ghost/note.txt and submit the code word in it with answer.
5-13.reveal: In ghost's home directory there's only a slip of paper: "ECHO-LIMA". The station roster has no such person, yet the login records show it comes online every night. An intruder, or something else?

hints: First type: umask 077
Then create a file: touch test.txt
Print the permission number with stat -c %a test.txt and answer it.
5-14.title: umask: Default Permissions
5-14.story:
A newly created file's starting permissions are decided by umask, a mask of "permissions to take away":
  files start at 666 (rw-rw-rw-), directories at 777
  subtract the umask to get the actual permissions
For example umask 022: file 666−022 = 644; umask 077: file 666−077 = 600 (only you can read and write).
Type umask NUMBER to set it (affects only this shell).
5-14.goal: In this shell run umask 077, then touch a new file, check its permissions with ls -l or stat -c %a, and submit that number with answer.

hints: The symbol for the sticky bit is t.
Type: sudo chmod +t /srv/drop
Or use numbers: sudo chmod 1777 /srv/drop; then ls -ld /srv/drop ends with a t.
5-15.title: The Sticky Bit
5-15.story:
A shared scratch directory like /tmp is writable by everyone. But then others could also delete files you put in it!

The sticky bit (shown as a final t in ls -l) fixes this: files in the directory can be deleted only by their owner (and root).
Set it with chmod +t dir, or with numbers by putting 1 in front of the permissions, e.g. 1777.
5-15.goal: /srv/drop is a world-writable inbox (777) without the sticky bit. Set it to 1777.

hints: The symbol for setgid is g+s.
Type: sudo chmod g+s /srv/team
Or directly: sudo chmod 2770 /srv/team; ls -ld /srv/team then shows an s in the group part.
5-16.title: Setgid Directories
5-16.story:
Shared team directories have an old problem: each person's new files belong to their own primary group, so teammates may be unable to read them.

Set setgid (symbol g+s) on the directory, and new files created inside automatically inherit "this directory's group".
Set it with chmod g+s dir, or with numbers by putting 2 in front, e.g. 2770.
5-16.goal: /srv/team belongs to group crew with permissions 770. Add setgid so it becomes 2770.

hints: Format: sudo setfacl -m u:user:perms file
The permission is rw and the user is cadet.
Type: sudo setfacl -m u:cadet:rw /srv/acl/report.txt, then check with getfacl /srv/acl/report.txt.
5-17.title: ACLs: Finer-Grained Access
5-17.story:
Traditional permissions have only three groups (owner, group, others), which isn't fine-grained enough. An ACL (Access Control List) can grant permissions to any specific user or group individually:
  setfacl -m u:user:perms file   add or modify (-m = modify; u means user)
  getfacl file                   show the current settings
For example u:cadet:rw means "user cadet, give rw".
5-17.goal: /srv/acl/report.txt belongs to root with permissions 640. Use setfacl to give the user cadet read and write (rw) without changing anyone else's permissions.

hints: First create the directory: sudo mkdir /srv/project
Then change its group to dev: sudo chgrp dev /srv/project (chgrp = change group)
Finally set the permissions: sudo chmod 3770 /srv/project (the leading 3 = setgid 2 + sticky 1).
5-18.title: Boss: The Team Shared Directory
5-18.story:
A dev team needs a shared directory /srv/project with these requirements:
  ① alice and bob (both in group dev) can read and write
  ② new files automatically belong to group dev (setgid, number 2)
  ③ they can't delete each other's files (sticky, number 1)
  ④ outsider carol can't enter at all (others get 0)

Combined: the special digit 3 (= 2+1) plus 770 (owner and group full control) = 3770.
Steps: create the directory → change its group to dev → set the permissions.
5-18.goal: Create /srv/project: group dev, permissions 3770 (setgid + sticky + full control for the group, nothing for others).
5-18.reveal: The shared directory is locked down, and Warden can no longer quietly change other people's files. You've held the first door, but the account called ghost still shows up on schedule every night.

hints: Type: ps aux | grep starlink to list lines containing starlink.
The 2nd column of the output is the PID (the 1st is the owner).
Lazy way: pgrep -x starlink-daemon prints the PID directly.
6-01.title: ps: Who's Running
6-01.story:
Every running program is a "process" to the system and has a unique number, its PID (process id).

ps lists processes. The most common form is ps aux: a and x show everyone's and all processes, and u makes the output more detailed. The output is very long, so it's usually combined with | grep keyword to keep only lines with the keyword.
The station has a resident program called starlink-daemon (a "daemon" is a service that keeps running in the background).
6-01.goal: Find starlink-daemon's PID and submit the number with answer.

hints: Type: ps aux | grep ledger
Look at column 1 of that line: that's the owner.
Advanced: get the PID with pgrep, then ps -o user= -p PID prints only the owner.
6-02.title: Whose Process Is It
6-02.story:
The first column USER in ps aux output is the process's "owner", i.e. whose permissions it runs with. Identity matters: if a program running as root misbehaves, the damage is far bigger than from an ordinary user.

ledger-writer is a background service. Find out which user runs it.
6-02.goal: Find the owner of the ledger-writer process and submit the user name with answer.

hints: Get the PID first: pgrep -x starlink-daemon
Format: kill PID (replace with the number you got)
If the PID is 1234 type kill 1234, then confirm with pgrep that it's gone.
6-03.title: kill: Ask It to Leave
6-03.story:
The command kill PID has a scary name but really "sends a signal to a process". By default it sends SIGTERM (number 15), meaning "please tidy up and quit"; the process can save and clean up before leaving, so it's polite.

starlink-daemon's shift is over: get its PID first, then kill it.
6-03.goal: Find starlink-daemon and end it with kill.

hints: Format: pkill processname
Type: pkill drone
Confirm with pgrep drone; no output means they're all gone.
6-04.title: pkill: Ending Many by Name
6-04.story:
Five drone processes have gone rogue. Looking up each PID and killing it one by one is too slow.

pkill name ends all processes with that name at once (killall name is similar). Make sure the name won't hit innocent processes before using it.

hints: Try plain pkill -f stubborn.sh first, then check with pgrep -f stubborn.sh whether it's still there.
If it's still there, force it: pkill -9 -f stubborn.sh
Or get the PID with pgrep -f stubborn.sh, then kill -9 PID.
6-05.title: SIGKILL: Forced Termination
6-05.story:
Some processes "catch" SIGTERM and pretend not to hear it, so plain kill does nothing.

Then use kill -9 (SIGKILL, number 9): this signal can't be caught, and the kernel just removes the process. It's a last resort, because the process gets no chance to save or clean up.
  pkill -9 -f keyword   find the process by its full command line and force-kill it
6-05.goal: stubborn.sh ignores ordinary kill. Find a way to end it.

hints: The & goes at the very end of the command.
Type: sleep 600 &
Then type jobs; you should see it Running.
6-06.title: Background Execution &
6-06.story:
Normally when you run a command you wait for it to finish before typing the next; that's running in the "foreground". Add an & at the end and it goes to the "background", returning the terminal to you at once.

The jobs command lists the work you've put in the background.
(sleep 600 means "sleep for 600 seconds", doing nothing, which is ideal for practice.)
6-06.goal: Start sleep 600 in the background (add & at the end).

hints: Type sleep 300 and press Enter; the terminal will wait for it to finish.
While it runs, hold Ctrl and press Z; you return to the prompt and see Stopped.
Type bg and Enter, then confirm with jobs that the state became Running.
6-07.title: Pause and Resume: Ctrl-Z, bg, fg
6-07.story:
When a program is running in the foreground and blocking your terminal, you can:
  Ctrl-Z   pause it (frozen, but not killed)
  bg       send the paused program to "keep running in the background"
  fg       bring a background program "back to the foreground"
  jobs     list all jobs and their states
It's like setting aside what you're doing so you can do something else.
6-07.goal: Run sleep 300, pause it with Ctrl-Z, then type bg to let it continue in the background.

hints: nohup goes at the very front and & at the very end.
Type: nohup sleep 500 &
Output goes to nohup.out; to discard it use: nohup sleep 500 > /dev/null 2>&1 &
6-08.title: nohup: Survive Logout
6-08.story:
When you close the terminal (or disconnect), the system sends a signal called SIGHUP ("hang up") to the programs under it, and they usually end with it.

If you run a long task and want it to survive closing the terminal, put nohup (no hang up) in front. Usually add & too, to run it in the background:
  nohup command &
Its output is saved automatically into nohup.out.
6-08.goal: Use nohup to run sleep 500 in the background.

hints: Type top, look at the top process, then press q to quit.
Or type: ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -5; the first entry (below the header) is the biggest CPU user.
Answer the name in its last column (COMMAND).
6-09.title: Who's Eating the CPU
6-09.story:
The engine is overheating; a process has eaten all the CPU (the computer's calculating brain). How do you find the culprit?
  top   a live screen that keeps updating, q to quit; the biggest CPU user is on top by default
  ps aux --sort=-%cpu   a one-time leaderboard, --sort=-%cpu meaning "order by CPU usage, highest first"
Add | head -5 to see only the top five.
6-09.goal: Find the name of the process with the highest CPU usage and submit it with answer.
6-09.reveal: The process eating all the CPU, cpu-hog, has exactly the same behavioral signature as Warden. It's "practicing", to hold up the whole station.

hints: Get the PID first: pgrep -x cpu-hog
Format: renice -n NUMBER -p PID
For example: renice -n 10 -p THE-PID-YOU-GOT.
6-10.title: nice and renice
6-10.story:
Don't want to kill the CPU hog, just ask it to be more polite? Adjust its nice value:
  nice values range from -20 to 19; the bigger the number, the politer and the lower its priority (others get the CPU first)
  renice -n NUMBER -p PID   adjust a process that's already running
6-10.goal: Raise cpu-hog's nice value to 10 or more (lowering its priority).

hints: Format: nice -n NUMBER command
To run in the background, don't forget the & at the end.
Type: nice -n 15 sleep 200 &
6-11.title: Be Polite from the Start
6-11.story:
The last level adjusted a program that was already running. To make it polite from the start, add nice when launching it:
  nice -n NUMBER command
Big, unhurried jobs like backups and compression are perfect for this, so they don't slow other things.
6-11.goal: Use nice with a value of 15 to run sleep 200 in the background.

hints: Type: free -m
Find the line starting with Mem:.
The total column (the first number after Mem:) is the total; answer it.
6-12.title: Memory and Load
6-12.story:
A few commands to check the system's "health":
  free -m     memory (RAM) usage, -m meaning units of MB
  uptime      how long it has been up, plus the "load average" (higher = busier)
  vmstat      an overview of resources
  watch -n SECONDS command   rerun a command every few seconds for simple live monitoring
6-12.goal: Use free -m to find this machine's total memory (MB, the first number on the Mem: line) and submit it with answer.

hints: Format: lsof filepath
Type: lsof /home/player/ledger.log
The 2nd column of the output (PID) is the answer.
6-13.title: lsof: Who Has This File Open
6-13.story:
In Linux "everything is a file": even network connections and devices are treated as files. lsof (list open files) shows "which files a process currently has open", and can also ask the reverse: "who has this file open right now?"

Use: when you try to delete or unmount something and are told it's "in use", this finds the process responsible.
ledger.log seems to be held by some process.
6-13.goal: Find the PID of the process that has ledger.log open and submit it with answer.

hints: Type: ss -tlnp
To see only 9000: ss -tlnp | grep 9000
At the end of that line find users:(("name",pid=NUMBER,...)) and answer the number after pid=.
6-14.title: Who's Holding This Port
6-14.story:
A new service fails to start with "Address already in use", meaning the "port" it wants (a numbered service window on the computer) has been taken by someone else.

ss -tlnp lists all network ports being "listened" on, and which process holds each:
  -t TCP only  -l listening only  -n numeric  -p show the process
With | grep 9000 you can find who uses port 9000.
6-14.goal: Find the PID of the process listening on port 9000 and submit it with answer.
6-14.reveal: The "diagnostic service" on port 9000 is fake. It's actually Warden's outside channel. It isn't attacking, it's calling for help.

hints: First type: timeout 1 sleep 5; it waits about 1 second and is stopped.
Right after, type: echo $? (run nothing else in between, or you'll see another command's result).
Answer the number printed.
6-15.title: timeout and Exit Codes
6-15.story:
Every command leaves an "exit code" when it ends: 0 means success, other numbers mean failure or special cases. Right after a command, echo $? shows the previous command's exit code ($? is a special variable holding it).

timeout SECONDS command gives a command a time limit and forcibly stops it when time is up, returning the special exit code 124. Great for preventing hangs.
6-15.goal: Run timeout 1 sleep 5 (a 5-second task given only 1 second), then immediately check the exit code with echo $? and submit that number with answer.

hints: In /proc/cpuinfo each core has a line starting with processor.
Type: grep -c ^processor /proc/cpuinfo (-c just counts the matching lines)
Even simpler: nproc prints the core count directly.
6-16.title: /proc: The Kernel's Window
6-16.story: /proc is a virtual directory the Linux kernel generates "on the fly". It doesn't hold real files; the kernel presents system information as files: each process has its own /proc/PID, CPU info is in /proc/cpuinfo, memory in /proc/meminfo. Reading them is like asking the kernel questions directly.
6-16.goal: Use /proc/cpuinfo to count how many processors (CPU cores) this machine has and submit the number with answer.

hints: cpu-hog can be handled directly: pkill cpu-hog
Find the PID holding port 9000: ss -tlnp | grep 9000 and read the number after pid=.
That process ignores ordinary kill, so force it: kill -9 PID.
Avoid over-broad commands (like a killall with no specific name); they would take starlink-daemon down too.
6-17.title: Boss: The Runaway Engine Room
6-17.story:
Alarms are blaring! cpu-hog has eaten the CPU, and a service is squatting on port 9000 and ignoring ordinary kill. But don't hurt starlink-daemon, the station's only communications program.

Use this stage's skills: pkill to kill by name, ss -tlnp to find who holds a port, kill -9 to force termination.
Principle: touch only the processes you should, and confirm the PID before acting.
6-17.goal: End cpu-hog and stop anything listening on port 9000, while keeping starlink-daemon running.
6-17.reveal: You shut down the runaway processes and the engine room went quiet. A line lit up on the terminal, sent by Warden: "...You finally came." It said nothing more, and did nothing more.

hints: Format: tar -cf archivename directory-to-pack
Type: tar -cf archive.tar docs
Use ls to confirm archive.tar appeared.
7-01.title: tar: Bundling
7-01.story:
When backing up a whole folder, sending files one by one is a chore. tar "packs" many files and directories into a single file (like putting things in a box; it just bundles, it doesn't shrink them yet).
  tar -cf boxname what-to-pack
Options: c is create, f is file (names the file; f must be immediately followed by the file name); add v (verbose) to watch the progress.
7-01.goal: Pack the docs directory into archive.tar.

hints: One more letter than last level: z (compress).
Format: tar -czf name.tar.gz directory
Type: tar -czf backup.tar.gz data
7-02.title: tar with Compression
7-02.story:
After packing you usually also "compress" to make the file smaller. Add a z to tar and it compresses with gzip as well; the usual extension is .tar.gz (or .tgz).
  tar -czf name.tar.gz what-to-pack
Mnemonic: c create, z compress, f file name.
7-02.goal: Pack the data directory, compress it with gzip, and save it as backup.tar.gz.

hints: First create the directory: mkdir restore
Peek at the contents: tar -tzf package.tar.gz
Unpack into it: tar -xzf package.tar.gz -C restore
7-03.title: tar: Extracting
7-03.story:
When you receive an archive, you need to "unpack" it:
  tar -xzf name.tar.gz   x is extract, z says it's gzip-compressed
  -C directory           where to unpack (capital C; the directory must already exist)
  tar -tzf name          t only lists the contents without unpacking (a peek first is good practice)
7-03.goal: package.tar.gz holds a set of files. Create the ~/restore directory first, then unpack it there.

hints: List the contents: tar -tf mystery.tar
Each item prints on one line, so the line count is the answer.
Type: tar -tf mystery.tar | wc -l and answer the number.
7-04.title: Peek Without Extracting
7-04.story:
When you get an archive of unknown origin, don't unpack it right away. tar -t "lists the contents without unpacking", so you can see what's inside first (it also avoids a "tar bomb", which spews a mass of files into your current directory when unpacked).
  tar -tf name.tar   list contents (a plain .tar needs no z)
7-04.goal: How many items (files and directories) are in mystery.tar? Without unpacking it, list and count with tar and submit the number with answer.

hints: Use gunzip to restore.
Format: gunzip file.gz
Type: gunzip notes.txt.gz, then ls shows notes.txt.
7-05.title: gzip and gunzip
7-05.story:
If you don't need packing and just want to compress a single file, use gzip directly:
  gzip file         compress; the original is replaced by file.gz
