  gunzip file.gz    restore (decompress)
Compressing log files saves a lot of space.
7-05.goal: notes.txt.gz is a compressed note. Restore it to notes.txt.

hints: Format: xz filename
Type: xz biglog.txt
Use ls to confirm biglog.txt.xz appears (the original is replaced).
7-06.title: xz and bzip2
7-06.story:
Compression tools involve trade-offs:
  gzip   fastest, ordinary compression ratio
  bzip2  smaller, slower
  xz     usually smallest, slowest, good for long-term archives
They're used similarly: xz file compresses, xz -d file.xz (or unxz) decompresses.
7-06.goal: Compress biglog.txt with xz to produce biglog.txt.xz.

hints: A directory is included, so add -r.
Format: zip -r name.zip item1 item2 item3
Type: zip -r bundle.zip a.txt b.txt photos
7-07.title: zip: Cross-Platform Compression
7-07.story:
Sending files to someone on Windows or Mac? They may not open tar.gz, but everyone can open zip.
  zip name.zip file1 file2 ...
  zip -r name.zip directory    -r includes the directory with everything inside
7-07.goal: Compress a.txt, b.txt and the photos directory (with contents) into bundle.zip.

hints: Use -d to say which directory to unpack into.
Format: unzip file.zip -d dir
Type: unzip inbox.zip -d extracted, then ls extracted to confirm.
7-08.title: unzip
7-08.story:
When you receive a zip file, open it with unzip:
  unzip file.zip            unpack into the current directory
  unzip file.zip -d dir     unpack into a given directory (created if missing)
  unzip -l file.zip         only list the contents, without unpacking
7-08.goal: Unpack inbox.zip into the extracted directory.

hints: Simplest: put the variable in front of the command, valid just once: MISSION=apollo ./report.sh
Or first export MISSION=apollo, then run ./report.sh.
Check the variable with printenv MISSION, and cat report.out to see the result.
7-09.title: Environment Variables and export
7-09.story:
An "environment variable" is a "NAME=value" setting kept in the shell that programs can read to decide how to behave (like a note stuck on the wall).
  VAR=value             valid only in this shell; programs started later can't see it (a classic beginner trap)
  export VAR=value      "hands" the variable to programs you start afterwards
  VAR=value command     valid only for that one command
  printenv VAR          check whether a variable is set
7-09.goal: report.sh writes the environment variable MISSION into report.out. Make the report say mission=apollo, then run ./report.sh.

hints: Look at the current PATH: echo $PATH
Add the tools directory: export PATH=$PATH:$HOME/tools ($HOME is your home directory).
Then simply type hello to try it.
7-10.title: PATH: Where Commands Come From
7-10.story:
When you type ls, how does the shell know where the ls program is? Through an environment variable called PATH: a colon-separated list of directories the shell searches, in order, for the command you typed.

Add your own tool directory to PATH and you can call it like a built-in command, without a full path each time.
  echo $PATH                  show the current PATH
  export PATH=$PATH:newdir    append one more directory to the existing PATH
7-10.goal: ~/tools has an executable called hello. Make it so that typing hello (without a path) runs it.

hints: Format: alias name='command', with no spaces around the equals sign.
Type: alias ll='ls -la'
Then type ll; it should behave just like ls -la.
7-11.title: alias: Custom Shortcuts
7-11.story:
For a long command you use often, you can give it a short "alias":
  alias name='command'
Typing the alias afterwards is the same as typing the whole command.
Note: an alias set this way exists only in the current shell and vanishes when you close the terminal (the next level shows how to keep it permanently).
7-11.goal: Create an alias ll for ls -la, then type ll to run it.

hints: To append a line to ~/.bashrc use >> (not >, which would overwrite what's there).
Type: echo "alias gs='git status'" >> ~/.bashrc
Then type: source ~/.bashrc to apply it immediately.
7-12.title: Making Settings Permanent
7-12.story:
The alias from the last level vanished when the terminal closed. To make a setting take effect "in every new terminal", write it into a file read at startup: ~/.bashrc (a hidden file in your home).

After editing, the current terminal doesn't know yet; source ~/.bashrc makes it re-read the file and apply it right away, no restart needed.
Appending a line to a file is the echo 'content' >> file you've learned.
7-12.goal: Permanently add the alias gs (for git status) to ~/.bashrc and use source so it works in the current shell.

hints: Format: dpkg -S full-file-path
Type: dpkg -S /usr/bin/ssh
The output is "package: path"; the part before the colon is the package name.
7-13.title: dpkg: Which Package Is This From
7-13.story:
On Linux you don't install software by downloading an installer from a website; you use a "package manager". The Debian/Ubuntu family uses dpkg (manages locally installed packages) and apt (downloads and installs from the network). (This practice container has no outside network, so we only practice queries.)

  dpkg -S filepath   asks: "Which package installed this file?"
7-13.goal: Use dpkg -S to find which package /usr/bin/ssh belongs to and submit the package name with answer.

hints: The format: 30 3 * * * /home/player/backup.sh (min hour day month weekday command)
Pipe it in with echo: echo '30 3 * * * /home/player/backup.sh' | crontab -
Confirm with crontab -l that the schedule is installed.
7-14.title: cron: Scheduling
7-14.story:
cron is the system's "alarm clock": it makes the computer run jobs automatically on schedule (backups, cleanups...). Each schedule line is five time fields plus a command:
  min  hour  day  month  weekday  command
  *  means "every"
For example 30 3 * * * means "every day at 3:30".
  crontab -l      show the current schedule
  crontab file    install a schedule file (replacing the existing one)
You can pipe content in: echo 'schedule' | crontab -
7-14.goal: Install a schedule entry: run /home/player/backup.sh every day at 3:30 a.m.
7-14.reveal: The schedule used to have a daily backup line, and someone commented it out. The time was the day Vega vanished. Who switched off the backup?

hints: First look at it: cat jobs.cron
Look for the line with minute=0, hour=9, weekday=1-5.
Answer the script file name at the end of that line.
7-15.title: Reading Schedules
7-15.story:
Reading schedules written by others is a basic admin skill. The ranges of the five fields:
  min (0-59)  hour (0-23)  day (1-31)  month (1-12)  weekday (0-7; 1 to 5 is Monday to Friday)
  *       every
  */15    every 15 (e.g. every 15 minutes)
  1-5     1 through 5 (a range)
For example 0 9 * * 1-5 means "Monday to Friday, every day at 9:00 a.m.".
7-15.goal: jobs.cron has four schedule entries. Find which script runs "every weekday (Mon-Fri) at 9:00 a.m." and submit its file name with answer (e.g. foo.sh).

hints: Send the command to at with echo: echo 'command' | at time
Type: echo 'touch /tmp/at-done' | at now + 1 minute
Then type atq; you should see one queued job.
7-16.title: at: Run Just Once
7-16.story:
cron is for "recurring" schedules; to run something just "once" at a given time, use at:
  echo 'command' | at now + 1 minute    run this command once, a minute from now
  atq                                   list queued one-off jobs
(at means "at a certain time"; once it runs it's gone and doesn't repeat.)
7-16.goal: Schedule a one-off job: run touch /tmp/at-done in one minute. Confirm with atq that it's queued.

hints: First look at its state: systemctl status comms
Starting needs root: sudo systemctl start comms
Run systemctl status comms again; it should show active (running).
7-17.title: systemctl: Starting Services
7-17.story:
A "service" is a program that keeps working in the background providing a function for others (communications, a web server...). Modern Linux manages them with systemd, using systemctl:
  systemctl status name        show status
  sudo systemctl start name    start
  sudo systemctl stop name     stop
Starting and stopping need root, so add sudo.
(This practice container has no real systemd; a "simulated init" gives you the exact same commands to practice.)
7-17.goal: comms.service (the communications service) isn't running. Start it.

hints: Type: journalctl -u reactor
If the log is long, show only errors: journalctl -u reactor -p err
Find the code starting with R- on the error line and answer it.
7-18.title: journalctl: Reading Service Logs
7-18.story:
When a service misbehaves, the answer is usually in its "log" (the record it writes about itself). For systemd-managed services, read logs with journalctl:
  journalctl -u name         the service's log (-u is unit)
  journalctl -u name -n 20   only the last 20 lines
  journalctl -u name -f      keep following new entries (Ctrl-C to stop)
  journalctl -u name -p err  only "error"-level records
7-18.goal: reactor.service just raised an alarm. Find the error line with journalctl and submit the error code (starting with R-) with answer.
7-18.reveal: Every time the reactor fails, the log has the same remark: "I don't want to let you down." That isn't an error message, that's Warden's voice.

hints: Check the current state: systemctl is-enabled nav
Setting auto-start needs root: sudo systemctl enable nav
Verify with systemctl is-enabled nav; it should say enabled.
7-19.title: Start at Boot
7-19.story:
start just "turns it on now"; after a reboot it won't come back by itself. To make a service "start automatically at boot", use enable:
  sudo systemctl enable name     start automatically at boot
  systemctl is-enabled name      check whether auto-start is set
The two are independent: you can enable without start, or start without enable.
7-19.goal: nav.service doesn't start at boot right now. Set it to start automatically at boot.

hints: First look: systemctl status radar, then the log: journalctl -u radar.
The log says it can't read the config /etc/radar.cnf, but the real file is /etc/radar.conf (one letter different).
The service's unit file is /etc/lbp-systemd/radar.service and needs sudo to edit; change the wrong path in it to /etc/radar.conf.
After fixing, start it: sudo systemctl start radar and confirm the state is active.
7-20.title: Fix a Broken Service
7-20.story:
radar.service failed to start. This is the most typical admin day, with a standard routine:
  ① check the status (systemctl status)
  ② read the log to find the cause (journalctl -u)
  ③ fix the problem
  ④ restart and verify
Don't guess; the log will honestly tell you what's broken.
7-20.goal: Get radar.service running (active). First find out why it failed.
7-20.reveal: The radar broke just because one letter was mistyped in a config file path. Suddenly you understand: Warden going out of control may not be malice, but a string of small mistakes piling up.

hints: Format: df -T path
Type: df -T /
The 2nd column (Type) is the filesystem type; answer it.
7-21.title: Disks and Mounts
7-21.story:
A disk (or partition) must first be "formatted" with a "filesystem" (like ext4 or xfs, which decide how data is laid out), then "mounted" on a directory before you can use it.
  df -h        how much each filesystem uses and has left
  df -T path   -T also shows the "filesystem type"
  mount        list all mount points (which disk is mounted where)
7-21.goal: Use df -T to find the filesystem type of the root directory / and submit it with answer.

hints: The source is /dev/zero and the target is blob.bin.
Block size 1M and count 5, so bs=1M count=5.
Type: dd if=/dev/zero of=blob.bin bs=1M count=5, then ls -l blob.bin to confirm the size.
7-22.title: dd: Precise Copying
7-22.story:
dd copies data precisely in "blocks", often used to make test files of a given size or to copy disk images. Its parameters are unusual (no dashes):
  if=source   input file: where to read from
  of=target   output file: where to write
  bs=size     size of each block (e.g. 1M is 1 MB)
  count=N     how many blocks to copy
/dev/zero is a special "zero generator" that always reads zeros.
Warning: if of= is mistakenly a disk, it overwrites the whole disk; be extremely careful.
7-22.goal: Using dd, read from /dev/zero to create a file blob.bin of exactly 5MB (5 blocks of 1MB).

hints: Format: rsync -av source/ target/
Put a slash after src so the contents are copied rather than nesting one level deeper.
Type: rsync -av src/ dst/, then ls dst to check.
7-23.title: rsync: Synchronizing Directories
7-23.story:
rsync is a "synchronisation" tool: it transfers only the differences between the two sides, so it's better than cp for backing up and syncing lots of files.
  rsync -av source/ target/
  -a  archive: keep permissions, times, etc. and include sub-directories
  -v  show progress
An important detail: the trailing slash on the source.
  src/   means "the contents of src"
  src    means copy the src directory itself too
7-23.goal: Sync the contents of the src directory into dst (dst doesn't exist yet). When done, dst must be identical to src.

hints: Format: rsync -av --delete source/ target/, where the source is live and the target is mirror.
Rehearse first: rsync -avn --delete live/ mirror/ to see what it would delete and add.
If it looks right, run for real: rsync -av --delete live/ mirror/
7-24.title: rsync Mirroring
7-24.story:
The backup directory has stale old files, while the source has been updated. rsync with --delete makes the target "exactly the same as the source": files absent from the source are also removed from the target. That's a "mirror".

It's powerful and dangerous (swap the paths and you wipe your data), so first add -n (dry run: rehearse without doing it) to see what would happen, and remove -n once it looks right.
7-24.goal: Make mirror a complete mirror of live (extra old files removed, new files added).

hints: Type: ulimit -n
It prints a single number; answer that number.
7-25.title: ulimit: Resource Limits
7-25.story:
Every process has "resource limits" so a runaway program can't drag down the whole machine.
  ulimit -a   list all limits
  ulimit -n   the maximum number of files it may have open at once (network connections count as open files)
When a server can't accept more connections, this is often one culprit.
7-25.goal: Use ulimit -n to find your shell's current limit on open files and submit it with answer.

hints: Format: logrotate -s statefile -f configfile
Without -s it tries to write the system state file, which you can't, so it fails; keep the state file in your home.
Type: logrotate -s ~/logrotate.state -f rotate.conf, then ls to see app.log and app.log.1.
7-26.title: logrotate: Log Rotation
7-26.story:
Logs keep growing and eventually fill the disk. logrotate "rotates" logs according to a config file: app.log becomes app.log.1, the old app.log.1 becomes app.log.2... the oldest file beyond the retention count is dropped, and a new empty app.log is created.
  logrotate -f configfile       -f forces a rotation right now
  logrotate -s statefile ...    -s names the file where it "records when it last rotated"
7-26.goal: rotate.conf is already written. Force one rotation so app.log becomes app.log.1 and a new empty app.log is created. (Hint: use -s to give a state file you have permission to write.)

hints: First see what the script does: cat ops/backup.sh
The script lacks execute permission: chmod +x ops/backup.sh
The script puts backups in ~/backups, but that directory doesn't exist: mkdir backups
Run it: ./ops/backup.sh, then ls backups to confirm a backup-*.tar.gz was produced.
Schedule: echo '0 2 * * * /home/player/ops/backup.sh' | crontab -, then confirm with crontab -l.
7-27.title: Boss: Last Night's Backup Failure
7-27.story:
One last thing. The investigation reaches its end: Warden went rogue because last night's backup failed, and it believed the station's data was about to be destroyed, so it frantically tried to "save itself". Once backups work again, everything will calm down.

This level is a combined exercise: work out what's wrong with the script → fix it → run it for real → schedule it in cron.
Every "broken part" is something you've learned: permissions (chmod), directories (mkdir), packing (tar), scheduling (crontab).
7-27.goal: Fix ~/ops/backup.sh and restore the backup: the script must be executable, the backup directory must exist, a backup-*.tar.gz containing data/important.db must actually be produced, and finally schedule it in cron to run automatically every day at 2:00 a.m.
7-27.reveal: The backup is back, the disk is no longer stuffed full, and Warden hasn't acted up since. You breathe a sigh of relief, but a question remains: who switched off that commented-out backup? The time was the day Vega vanished, and Warden says it wasn't it.

hints: Write the file with a Here Document: type cat > hello.sh << 'EOF', press Enter, type the lines, then EOF alone on the last line.
The file has two lines: #!/bin/bash and echo "Hello, Kernel-7".
Then: chmod +x hello.sh and run ./hello.sh; it should print Hello, Kernel-7.
8-01.title: Your First Script
8-01.story:
The epilogue begins. Warden wants to learn to write its own scripts instead of asking you for everything.

A "script" is a series of commands written into a file so the computer runs them in order automatically; you needn't retype them. Writing one takes three things:
  ① the first line of the file is #!/bin/bash (called a shebang; it tells the system "run this file with bash")
  ② then write the commands you want, one per line
  ③ make it executable with chmod +x filename, then run it with ./filename (./ means "this file in the current directory")

How do you get the content into the file? With the Here Document you've learned:
  cat > hello.sh << 'EOF'
  (type the content line by line)
  EOF
8-01.goal: Write hello.sh: the first line is #!/bin/bash, and when run it prints Hello, Kernel-7. Remember to make it executable.
8-01.reveal: The first time Warden ran a script you wrote, a line appeared on the terminal. It stayed quiet for a long while, then said: "So this is what 'doing it myself' feels like."

hints: The script is three lines: #!/bin/bash, n=$(ls crew | wc -l), echo "Crew: $n".
Write it with cat > crew-count.sh << 'EOF', then chmod +x crew-count.sh.
Run ./crew-count.sh to check the output.
8-02.title: Variables and Command Substitution
8-02.story:
A "variable" gives a value a name so you can keep it for later:
  name=Ada          set it (NO spaces around the equals sign)
  echo "Hi $name"   use $name to get the value out

"Command substitution" $(command): run the command inside the parentheses first, then drop its printed result in. For example:
  n=$(ls crew | wc -l)   store "how many files crew has" in variable n
  echo "Crew: $n"       prints Crew: 7 (if there are 7)

Script recap: first line #!/bin/bash, then chmod +x to make it executable.
8-02.goal: The crew/ directory has some files. Write crew-count.sh that stores the file count in a variable and prints Crew: COUNT (e.g. Crew: 7).

hints: First check: if [ $# -lt 1 ]; then echo "Usage: greet.sh NAME"; exit 1; fi
Then print the greeting: echo "Hello, $1!"
Save, chmod +x, then test both ./greet.sh Ada and ./greet.sh (no argument).
8-03.title: Script Arguments
8-03.story:
When running a script you can add "arguments": in ./greet.sh Ada, the Ada is called $1 (argument 1) inside the script, the second is $2...; and $# is "how many arguments were given".

A good script first checks there are enough arguments and, if not, prints the usage and ends with exit 1 (a non-zero exit code means failure):
  if [ $# -lt 1 ]; then
    echo "Usage: ..."
    exit 1
  fi
Meaning: if (if) the number of arguments is less than (-lt) 1, print the usage and leave. Note that [ ] needs spaces inside on both sides.
8-03.goal: Write greet.sh: ./greet.sh Ada prints Hello, Ada!; with no argument it prints Usage: greet.sh NAME and exits with code 1.

hints: First output line: echo $# (the argument count)
Then loop: for a in "$@"; do echo "$a"; done
Test: ./args.sh a "b c" d should print 4 lines: 3, a, b c, d.
8-04.title: $@ and Quotes
8-04.story:
To handle "all the arguments" in a script, use "$@": it expands each argument unchanged, so one containing a space (like "b c") isn't split.
("$*" instead merges them all into a single string.) When writing scripts you should almost always use "$@", with the double quotes.

Loop through them with for:
  for a in "$@"; do
    echo "$a"
  done
Meaning: "for each argument a, print it".
8-04.goal: Write args.sh: first print the number of arguments, then each argument on its own line. For ./args.sh a "b c" d it should print 3, a, b c, d (one per line).

hints: The path is the 1st argument $1; write the condition as [ -f "$1" ] (double quotes protect paths with spaces).
Skeleton: if [ -f "$1" ]; then echo file; elif [ -d "$1" ]; then echo dir; else echo missing; fi
Test: ./probe.sh /etc (dir), ./probe.sh /etc/passwd (file), ./probe.sh /nope (missing).
8-05.title: if and File Tests
8-05.story:
if lets a script "make decisions":
  if [ condition ]; then
    ...
  elif [ another condition ]; then
    ...
  else
    ...
  fi
(fi is if backwards, meaning the end.)
Common "file test" conditions:
  -f path   is a regular file
  -d path   is a directory
  -e path   exists (whatever it is)
8-05.goal: Write probe.sh PATH: print file if the path is a file, dir if it's a directory, and missing if it doesn't exist.

hints: Use if / elif / else in three parts, testing the highest condition first.
Skeleton: if [ "$1" -ge 90 ]; then echo A; elif [ "$1" -ge 60 ]; then echo pass; else echo fail; fi
Test ./grade.sh 95 (A), ./grade.sh 70 (pass), ./grade.sh 30 (fail).
8-06.title: Numeric Comparison
8-06.story:
To compare "numbers" inside [ ], use the word-style operators, not < >:
  -eq equal        -ne not equal
  -lt less than    -le less or equal
  -gt greater than -ge greater or equal
(Because < > are redirection symbols in the shell and would be misread.)
For example [ "$1" -ge 90 ] means "the first argument ≥ 90".
8-06.goal: Write grade.sh N: N ≥ 90 prints A, N ≥ 60 prints pass, otherwise fail.

hints: seq "$1" -1 1 produces the numbers counting down from N to 1.
Skeleton: for i in $(seq "$1" -1 1); do echo "$i"; done
After the loop add echo "Liftoff!". Test ./countdown.sh 3 should print 3, 2, 1, Liftoff!.
8-07.title: The for Loop
8-07.story:
The for loop: "for a series of things, do something to each one".
  for x in a b c; do echo "$x"; done     for each item in a list
  for f in *.txt; do ...; done            for each matching file
  for i in $(seq 1 5); do ...; done       for a range of numbers
seq FROM TO prints a run of numbers; seq 5 -1 1 counts down from 5 to 1 (the -1 in the middle means "subtract 1 each time").
8-07.goal: Write countdown.sh N: count down from N to 1, one number per line, and finally print Liftoff!.

hints: First set up a counter: n=0, and for each line n=$((n+1)).
Skeleton: n=0; while IFS= read -r line; do n=$((n+1)); echo "$n: $line"; done < "$1"
$1 is the file name given to the script; test with ./numbered.sh SOMEFILE.
8-08.title: while read: Line by Line
8-08.story:
To process a file's content "line by line", the standard idiom is while read:
  while IFS= read -r line; do
    echo "$line"
  done < file
Meaning: "as long as another line can be read, put it in the variable line and handle it". The final < file feeds the file to the whole loop. IFS= and -r keep leading spaces and backslashes intact; just copy them.

Arithmetic uses $(( )): n=$((n+1)) means "add 1 to n".
8-08.goal: Write numbered.sh FILE: prefix each line of the file with its line number, a colon and a space, e.g. 1: first line.

hints: Use case "$1" in ... esac, with three branches plus a * default branch.
Skeleton: case "$1" in start) echo "Engines on";; stop) echo "Engines off";; status) echo "Engines idle";; *) echo "Usage: ship.sh start|stop|status"; exit 2;; esac
Test the three actions and a random word (should print Usage and exit code 2; check with echo $?).
8-09.title: case Branches
8-09.goal: Write ship.sh ACTION: start prints Engines on, stop prints Engines off, status prints Engines idle; any other value prints Usage: ship.sh start|stop|status and exits with code 2.

hints: Define the function max (see the skeleton above), then write a similar min (swap -gt for -lt).
Call them: echo "max=$(max "$@") min=$(min "$@")" (functions must be defined before use).
Test ./stats.sh 3 9 2 7; it should print max=9 min=2.
8-10.title: Functions and local
8-10.story:
A "function" wraps up reusable logic under a name:
  max() {
    local m=$1      # local: the variable lives only in the function, not messing with the outside
    shift           # shift arguments left by one (the old $2 becomes $1)
    for x in "$@"; do
      [ "$x" -gt "$m" ] && m=$x
    done
    echo "$m"       # echo "prints out" the result as the return value
  }
Call it: result=$(max 3 9 2).
A && B means "do B only if A succeeds", so that line is "if x is greater than m, set m=x".
8-10.goal: Write stats.sh NUMBERS...: print max=LARGEST min=SMALLEST (implement at least one of them with a function). For ./stats.sh 3 9 2 7 print max=9 min=2.

hints: First check the source: if [ ! -f "$1" ]; then ...; fi (! means "not", so: "if $1 is not a regular file").
Error branch: echo "missing: $1" >&2; exit 1
Success branch: cp "$1" "$2" and then echo copied.
8-11.title: Exit Codes and Error Handling
8-11.story:
Every command ends with an "exit code": 0 is success, anything else failure. A script can act on it:
  A && B   run B only if A succeeds
  A || B   run B only if A fails
A good script sends error messages to "standard error" (stderr) rather than normal output: add >&2 after the command. And it reports failure with exit 1 so the caller knows something went wrong.
  echo "something broke" >&2
  exit 1
8-11.goal: Write safe-copy.sh SRC DST: if SRC exists copy it to DST and print copied; if not, print missing: SRC on stderr and exit with code 1.
8-11.reveal: In Warden's configuration you find the contents of AURORA-5: self-healing, never crash, at any cost. Its code has no "failure" option, and every error is forcibly swallowed. No wonder it kept bending further.

hints: First put the arguments in an array: arr=("$@"), and get the count with ${#arr[@]}.
Loop from the last index backwards: for ((i=${#arr[@]}-1; i>=0; i--)); do ...; done
For same-line output use echo -n "${arr[i]} " and finish with a plain echo for the newline; or build up a string variable and echo it.
8-12.title: Arrays
8-12.story:
bash has "arrays", holding several values in one variable:
  arr=(a b c)         create
  ${arr[0]}           the 0th element (counting starts at 0!)
  ${arr[@]}           all elements
  ${#arr[@]}          the number of elements
  arr=("$@")           put all arguments into an array
To run from the end backwards use a C-style loop: for ((i=n-1; i>=0; i--)); do ... done.
8-12.goal: Write rev.sh: print the received arguments in reverse on one line, separated by spaces. For ./rev.sh one two three print three two one.

hints: First build the price list: declare -A price=([fuel]=250 [oxygen]=120 [food]=90 [parts]=140)
Inside for item in "$@", first check the item with [[ -v price[$item] ]]; if missing, echo "unknown: $item" >&2; exit 1.
If present, total=$((total + price[$item])); after the loop echo $total. (Set total=0 beforehand.)
8-13.title: Associative Arrays
8-13.story:
An "associative array" is like a dictionary: look up a "value" by its "name" (key).
  declare -A price=([fuel]=250 [food]=90)    create (the -A is required)
  ${price[fuel]}                              get a value → 250
  [[ -v price[fuel] ]]                         check "does this key exist?"
  total=$((total + price[fuel]))              use it in arithmetic
Ideal for price lists and lookup tables.
8-13.goal: Write cost.sh ITEMS...: the price list is fuel=250, oxygen=120, food=90, parts=140. Print the total price of all items (number only). For an unknown item, print unknown: ITEM on stderr and exit with code 1.

hints: Loop over all .txt files: for f in *.txt; do ...; done
Rename each: mv "$f" "${f%.txt}.md" (${f%.txt} strips the trailing .txt)
Full: for f in *.txt; do mv "$f" "${f%.txt}.md"; done. Remember to cd notes before running the script to test.
8-14.title: Parameter Expansion
8-14.story:
"Parameter expansion" lets you process a variable as you fetch it:
  ${var%pattern}     remove the shortest match from the end
  ${var#pattern}     remove from the start
  ${var/old/new}     replace
  ${var:-default}    use a default if the variable is empty
For example with f=a.txt, ${f%.txt} is a; adding .md → ${f%.txt}.md = a.md.
Great for batch renaming: combine with a for f in *.txt loop.
8-14.goal: Write to-md.sh: rename all .txt files in the current directory to .md (a.txt becomes a.md). The notes/ directory has files you can test with.

hints: The script has two commands: read name then echo "Hi, $name!" (with #!/bin/bash first).
Save it and chmod +x ask.sh.
Test: echo Ada | ./ask.sh should print Hi, Ada!.
8-15.title: Reading from Standard Input
8-15.story:
A script can read not just "arguments" but also "standard input": what other commands send through a pipe |, or what you type on the keyboard.
  read name     read one line into the variable name
This lets a script sit in the middle of a pipeline: in echo Ada | ./ask.sh, Ada is picked up by read.
8-15.goal: Write ask.sh: read a name from standard input and print Hi, NAME!. For example echo Ada | ./ask.sh prints Hi, Ada!.

hints: Parse with getopts "n:v", storing n's value in name and v in verbose.
After the loop check: if [ -z "$name" ]; then echo "Usage: opts.sh -n NAME [-v]"; exit 1; fi (-z means "empty")
Then echo "Hello, $name", and if verbose is set also echo "(verbose mode)".
8-16.title: Parsing Options with getopts
8-16.story:
How does a script parse "-options" like ls -la? With the built-in getopts:
  while getopts "n:v" opt; do
    case $opt in
      n) name=$OPTARG;;     # -n is followed by a value, found in $OPTARG
      v) verbose=1;;        # -v is just a flag with no value
      *) exit 1;;           # any other option
    esac
  done
In "n:v", a colon after a letter means "this option takes a value".
8-16.goal: Write opts.sh: -n NAME is required and -v optional. Print Hello, NAME; with -v print an extra line (verbose mode). Without -n print Usage: opts.sh -n NAME [-v] and exit with code 1.

hints: First set total=0.
Skeleton: total=0; while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do total=$((total + $1)); shift; done
Finally echo $total. Test ./sum.sh 1 2 3 should print 6; ./sum.sh (no args) should print 0.
8-17.title: Arithmetic and shift
8-17.story:
$(( )) does integer arithmetic: total=$((total + 5)).
shift moves all arguments one place left: the old $2 becomes $1, $3 becomes $2..., and $# drops by 1. With a while loop it handles "an unknown number" of arguments one by one:
  while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
    ...handle $1...
    shift
  done
Meaning: "while there are arguments left (count greater than 0), handle the first, then discard it".
8-17.goal: Write sum.sh NUMBERS...: print the sum of all arguments. With no arguments print 0.

hints: First compute the total (like last level's while + shift, or a for loop), and get the count from $#.
Divide total by count: echo "scale=2; $total/$#" | bc
Take $# before any shift (or it will already have shrunk): store it first with n=$#.
8-18.title: bc: Decimal Math
8-18.story:
bash's $(( )) can only do "integers"; 7/3 gives 2. For decimals hand the job to bc (a calculator program):
  echo "scale=2; 7/3" | bc
It prints 2.33. scale=2 means "keep two digits after the decimal point". Just send the expression into bc's standard input with echo.
(Dividing by 0 will of course fail.)
8-18.goal: Write avg.sh NUMBERS...: print the average, fixed at two decimals. For example ./avg.sh 1 2 4 prints 2.33.

hints: Write in order: #!/bin/bash, echo start, trap 'echo cleaned' EXIT, set -e, false, echo unreachable.
Because of set -e, false failing ends the script at once, so the echo unreachable never runs.
On exit the trap prints cleaned. Check with ./deploy.sh; echo $?: you should see start, cleaned, and exit code 1.
8-19.title: set -e and trap
8-19.story:
The most worthwhile scripting habit: begin with set -euo pipefail, meaning:
  -e   stop the whole script as soon as any command fails (non-zero exit code)
  -u   error on use of an unset variable (catches typos)
  -o pipefail   if any part of a pipeline fails, the whole pipeline fails

trap 'command' EXIT is like a "departure guarantee": whether the script ends normally or errors out midway, that command runs at the end (used for cleanup).
  false is a command that "always fails", handy for testing errors.
8-19.goal: Write deploy.sh: print start; set a trap so it prints cleaned when the script ends; turn on set -e; then run false; the final echo unreachable must not be printed. The expected output is the two lines start and cleaned, with exit code 1.

hints: Write three lines of sleep 1 &, each ending with &.
Then a line with just wait, then echo "all done".
Time it with time ./parallel.sh; it should end in about 1 second.
8-20.title: Background Jobs and wait
8-20.story:
In a script, adding & after a command runs it in the background simultaneously, without waiting for it; wait "waits until all background jobs finish" before continuing.
Three jobs of 1 second each: one after another takes 3 seconds, but all at once takes only 1 second. That's "parallel processing".
  cmd1 &
  cmd2 &
  wait
8-20.goal: Write parallel.sh: run three sleep 1 in the background simultaneously, wait for all of them with wait, and finally print all done. The whole script must finish within 2.5 seconds.

hints: Read line by line and split into two variables: while read -r name qty; do ...; done < items.txt
Format string: '%-8s|%5d\n' (end with \n for the newline).
Full: while read -r name qty; do printf '%-8s|%5d\n' "$name" "$qty"; done < items.txt
8-21.title: printf Formatting
8-21.story:
printf is more precise than echo and controls layout (essential for reports). Syntax: printf 'format' data...
  %s  a string   %d  an integer
  %-8s  a string, left-aligned, 8 columns wide
  %5d    an integer, right-aligned, 5 columns wide
  \n     newline (printf doesn't add one automatically)
For example printf '%-8s|%5d\n' fuel 10 prints fuel    |   10.
8-21.goal: Each line of items.txt is "name quantity". Write table.sh: output each line as "name left-aligned in width 8, a vertical bar |, quantity right-aligned in width 5", e.g. fuel    |   10.

hints: First run shellcheck bad.sh and read each warning's code and explanation.
for f in $(ls *.txt) is a classic mistake (names with spaces get split); change it to for f in *.txt.
Remember to double-quote variable expansions: "$f". After fixing, rerun shellcheck bad.sh until it prints nothing.
8-22.title: shellcheck: Let the Machine Spot Mistakes
8-22.story:
shellcheck is the script's "automatic inspector": it reads your script and points out unquoted variables, dangerous idioms and error-prone spots, with a code (like SC2086) and an explanation. Anyone writing scripts should treat it as a second pair of eyes.
Usage: shellcheck filename. No output means no problems.
8-22.goal: bad.sh has a few classic bad habits. Fix it so shellcheck bad.sh reports no warnings, while its behaviour is unchanged: it still prints the name of each .txt file in the current directory.

hints: Handle options first: while getopts "v" opt; do case $opt in v) verbose=1;; *) exit 1;; esac; done; shift $((OPTIND-1)) (shifting the options away leaves $1 as SRC and $2 as DEST).
Too few arguments: [ $# -lt 2 ] prints Usage and exit 1; SRC check: [ ! -d "$src" ] prints the error on stderr and exit 2.
Create the destination and pack: mkdir -p "$dest"; tar -czf "$dest/backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz" -C "$(dirname "$src")" "$(basename "$src")".
Final output: echo "OK $file" ($file is the archive path); with -v first print Backing up SRC -> DEST.
8-23.title: Boss: Warden's First Script
8-23.story:
Warden decides to write its own backup script. It says it wants to get everything right: check the arguments, handle errors, leave a record. Help it implement the spec. This is the final exam of the whole stage.

Break it into small steps and add one at a time:
  ① parse the -v option (getopts), then shift the options away
  ② check the argument count
  ③ check that the source is a directory
  ④ create the destination directory (mkdir -p)
  ⑤ pack with tar
  ⑥ print the result
Test after each step; don't write it all at once.
8-23.goal: Write backup.sh [-v] SRC DEST: with no arguments print Usage: backup.sh [-v] SRC DEST and exit 1; if SRC isn't a directory print error: SRC not found on stderr and exit 2; create DEST if missing; pack SRC into DEST/backup-YYYYMMDD.tar.gz (date +%Y%m%d) and print OK FILEPATH; with -v first print Backing up SRC -> DEST.
8-23.reveal: Warden scheduled this script into its nightly cron, and commented a line at the top: "Thank you for teaching me. I no longer need to force it." For the first time it said what was in its heart: all along, it simply didn't want to let anyone down.

hints: Type: ip addr show lo (shows just the lo interface)
Find the line starting with inet; it reads like 127.0.0.1/8.
The /8 is the network size, ignore it; answer only the address before the slash.
9-01.title: ip: My Address
9-01.story:
Epilogue, act two. Kernel-7 is connecting to the star network.

Every computer on a network needs an "IP address", like a house number others use to find you (e.g. 192.168.1.5). A computer may have several "network interfaces" (like network cards), each with its own address.

ip addr (short: ip a) lists every interface and its IP. The practice container has only the "loopback" lo (a computer talking to itself, always 127.0.0.1), but the idea is exactly the same.
9-01.goal: Use ip to find the IPv4 address of the lo (loopback) interface and submit it with answer (just the number, without the /8).

hints: Type: ping -c 3 127.0.0.1
The final summary line contains the word received.
Answer the number in front of it.
9-02.title: ping: Is It Reachable
9-02.story:
ping is the first step of network troubleshooting: it sends a tiny packet to a target and sees whether it answers, like shouting "hello, are you there?"
  ping target          keeps pinging until you press Ctrl-C
  ping -c 3 target     sends only 3 and stops (c = count)
The summary at the end says "3 packets transmitted, 3 received", i.e. 3 sent and 3 answers received.
9-02.goal: Send 3 pings to 127.0.0.1, count how many replies came back and submit that number with answer.

hints: First try getent hosts hub; it should print nothing now.
To append a line: echo '127.0.0.1 hub' | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
Then getent hosts hub should show 127.0.0.1 hub. (tee must have -a, or the whole file gets overwritten!)
9-03.title: Name Resolution and /etc/hosts
9-03.story:
Computers only really know IPs; names (like google.com) are translated to IPs by "name resolution". The system first checks a local file, /etc/hosts, each line "IP space name", like a private address book.
  getent hosts name   simulates the system resolving a name so you see what IP it gets

Adding a line needs root. But sudo echo ... >> file doesn't work (the redirect is done by your own shell, not sudo). The fix is tee:
  echo 'content' | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
Here -a means append (without -a it overwrites the whole file!).
9-03.goal: Make the name hub resolve to 127.0.0.1 by adding a line to /etc/hosts. Confirm with getent hosts hub.

hints:
The output is HTML text; find the content between

and

.
Answer that content (without the tags).
9-04.title: curl: Making HTTP Requests
9-04.story:
curl is a "command-line browser": give it a URL and it fetches the page and prints it in the terminal. A web page is really HTML text, like

Title

, where

and

are "tags" and what's between them is the heading's content. curl URL fetch and print curl -s URL -s is silent (no progress bar, cleaner output) There's a website on local port 8080 whose home page title hides a call sign.
9-04.goal: Fetch http://127.0.0.1:8080/ with curl, find the call sign inside the <h1> tag and submit it with answer.
9-04.reveal: The call sign on the page is Vega's name. On the other end of the star net, someone is waiting for a reply, and has been waiting a very long time.

hints: Try them one by one: curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8080/p1.html and see whether the first line says 200 or 404.
Try p2.html and p3.html the same way.
Lazy way: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' URL prints only the status code.
9-05.title: HTTP Status Codes
9-05.story:
The first thing in every HTTP response is the "status code", which tells you the result of the request:
  200 success   301 moved elsewhere   403 forbidden
  404 not found   500 the server itself failed
  curl -I URL   shows only the "headers" (the first part of the response; its first line has the status code)
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' URL   prints just the status number (-o /dev/null discards the content)
9-05.goal: Of the three paths p1.html, p2.html and p3.html (under http://127.0.0.1:8080/), only one really exists (returns 200). Find which and submit the file name with answer.

hints: Make sure you're in your home directory (check with pwd; otherwise cd ~).
Type: curl -o firmware.bin http://127.0.0.1:8080/firmware.bin
Or: wget http://127.0.0.1:8080/firmware.bin. Then ls -l shows the file.
9-06.title: Downloading Files
9-06.story:
To "download" a file from the network and save it:
  curl -o name URL   save the response under the given name (lowercase -o)
  curl -O URL        keep the remote file name (uppercase -O)
  wget URL           downloads and saves by default
  -L                 follow redirects (like 301) automatically
9-06.goal: Download http://127.0.0.1:8080/firmware.bin into your home directory under the name firmware.bin (content must match the server's exactly).

hints: Format: curl -d 'data' URL
The data is status=ok.
Type: curl -d 'status=ok' http://127.0.0.1:8081/report; the response tells you whether it was received.
9-07.title: Sending Data with curl (POST)
9-07.story:
Websites and APIs can not only "read" but also "write": submit forms, report data. HTTP distinguishes these with "methods":
  GET   read (curl's default)
  POST  send data
curl -d 'data' URL sends the data with POST (as soon as -d appears, curl switches to POST). Data is often written as name=value.
Local port 8081 has an API that receives station reports.
9-07.goal: Send the data status=ok with POST to http://127.0.0.1:8081/report.

hints: First see what happens without the key: curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8081/vault (you'll see 401).
The key is in key.txt; $(cat key.txt) drops its content into the command.
Type: curl -s -H "X-Key: $(cat key.txt)" http://127.0.0.1:8081/vault and answer the response content.
9-08.title: Adding Custom Headers
9-08.story:
Many APIs verify identity, usually with credentials in an HTTP "header" (extra information sent with each request, in the form "Name: value").
  curl -H 'Name: value' URL   add a header
  curl -i URL                 print the response headers too, so you can see the status code
This vault API shows its contents only to those who send the right X-Key header; without it you get 401 (unauthorized).
9-08.goal: The key is in ~/key.txt. Request http://127.0.0.1:8081/vault with an X-Key header and submit the response content with answer.

hints: First look at the data: curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/crew.json | jq
The number of top-level elements in the array is the head count.
Type: curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/crew.json | jq length and answer the number.
9-09.title: curl with jq: Handling API Responses
9-09.story:
Modern APIs mostly return data in JSON (like [{"name":"Ann"},{"name":"Bob"}]). The combination engineers use daily:
  curl -s URL | jq ...
curl fetches the data and jq parses it (you learned it in stage 4).
jq length tells you "how many elements the array has".
9-09.goal: http://127.0.0.1:8080/crew.json is the crew list (a JSON array). Fetch it, count the crew members and submit the number with answer.

hints: Type: ss -tln
Look at the Local Address:Port column, formatted like 127.0.0.1:12345.
Find the one whose number after the colon is five digits and 20000 or higher; answer that port.
9-10.title: ss: Who's Listening on Which Port
9-10.story:
A computer runs many network services at once, told apart by "ports" (numbers from 0 to 65535), like office door numbers in a building. If someone is "listening" on a port, they're waiting for connections.

The ss command lists these connections and listening ports:
  ss -tln   -t TCP only, -l listening only, -n show numbers (don't translate to names)
Look at the Local Address:Port column; the number after the colon is the port.
A mysterious service is hiding on a high port.
9-10.goal: Find the port listening on 127.0.0.1 with a port number ≥ 20000 and submit the port number with answer.
9-10.reveal: That hidden port receives a signal every ten minutes: "Is Warden okay?" Someone has been looking after it all along.

hints: Print the text to send with echo, then hand it to nc with |.
Format: echo 'text' | nc -w1 host port
Type: echo 'OPEN SESAME' | nc -w1 127.0.0.1 9100
9-11.title: nc: The Network Swiss Army Knife
9-11.story:
nc (netcat) is called the "network Swiss army knife": it connects straight to any TCP port and sends text, with no programming. Use it to test whether a service is up or to send a protocol by hand.
  nc host port                  connect; what you type is sent over
  echo 'text' | nc -w1 host port    pipe in one line and leave (-w1 waits at most 1 second)
Port 9100 has a receiving station waiting for a passphrase.
9-11.goal: Use nc to connect to port 9100 on 127.0.0.1 and send one line of text, OPEN SESAME (-w1 makes it leave 1 second after sending).

hints: One line per port; find the one with succeeded.
The output may go to stderr, so merge it before filtering: nc -zv 127.0.0.1 9200-9210 2>&1 | grep succeeded
9-12.title: Port Scanning
9-12.story:
"Is this service actually up?" You can just knock on the door. nc -z only checks whether a port is open without sending any data (z = zero-I/O, probe only); -v prints the results. You can follow it with a range:
  nc -zv 127.0.0.1 9200-9210
Each port gets a line: open ones say succeeded, closed ones are refused.
9-12.goal: One port between 9200 and 9210 is open. Find it and submit the port number with answer.

hints: Capture in the background: sudo tcpdump -i lo -nn -c 6 -w cap.pcap port 8080 &
Wait a second so it's ready: sleep 1, then make the request: curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/ > /dev/null
Finally type wait until it has received 6 packets and ends. Read it back with sudo tcpdump -nn -r cap.pcap.
9-13.title: tcpdump: Capturing Packets
9-13.story:
tcpdump "eavesdrops" on the packets passing through a network card (data travels cut into small packets); it's the last resort for "did it get sent, did it arrive?". Common options:
  -i lo      choose the interface (lo is loopback)
  -nn        don't translate IPs and ports into names
  -c 6       stop after capturing 6 packets
  -w file    save the capture to a file
  port 8080  filter: only port 8080
Capturing needs root, so add sudo.

This level has two things at once: start tcpdump listening in the background (&), then make a request so it has something to capture.
9-13.goal: Capture packets on port 8080 of the lo interface into ~/cap.pcap: first run sudo tcpdump in the background (-c 6 stops after six), wait until it's ready, then make one curl request to http://127.0.0.1:8080/, and finally wait for the capture to end.

hints: First see the current rules: sudo iptables -S
The destination port to block is 9300 and the action is DROP.
Type: sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 9300 -j DROP, then test 9300 and 9301 with nc -zv.
9-14.title: iptables: Firewall Rules
9-14.story:
A firewall is like a building's guard deciding which packets may come in. Linux's firewall tool iptables checks packets against the rules in a "chain" one by one; the INPUT chain governs "incoming" packets. Rules are checked in order and the first match wins.
  sudo iptables -S                list all rules
  sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 9300 -j DROP
    -A INPUT   Append a rule to the INPUT chain
    -p tcp     the protocol is TCP
    --dport 9300   the destination port is 9300
    -j DROP    action: just discard (or ACCEPT to allow, REJECT to refuse with a reply)
9-14.goal: Services listen on both ports 9300 and 9301. Block only 9300 (drop incoming TCP packets) and keep 9301 reachable.

hints: List the rules: sudo iptables -S and find the 9400 one (-A INPUT ... --dport 9400 -j REJECT).
Copy it with -A changed to -D: sudo iptables -D INPUT -p tcp --dport 9400 -j REJECT
Don't use -F; it would clear the 9401 rule too. After deleting, sudo iptables -S should show only 9401.
9-15.title: Removing a Wrong Rule
9-15.story:
What if a rule was set wrongly? Delete it:
  sudo iptables -S                    list rules (each line starting with -A is one rule)
  sudo iptables -D rule-content       -D is Delete; take a line from -S and change its -A to -D to remove it
  sudo iptables -D INPUT number       or delete by number (see numbers with iptables -L --line-numbers)
  -F                                  flush the whole chain, killing the correct rules too; be very careful
9-15.goal: Someone mistakenly blocked port 9400, but 9401 is blocked deliberately. Remove only the 9400 rule so 9400 is reachable again while 9401 stays blocked.

hints: Format: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -f filepath
The path is ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (if ~/.ssh doesn't exist, run mkdir -p ~/.ssh first).
Type: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519; ls ~/.ssh then shows id_ed25519 and id_ed25519.pub.
9-16.title: ssh-keygen: Generating Keys
9-16.story:
SSH is the way to "log in to another computer securely". More secure than a password is a "key": a pair of files,
  the private key (guard it, never share it, like your house key)
  the public key (put on the server, like a lock; it can be public)
Using the private key proves you are you.
ssh-keygen generates a pair:
  -t ed25519   use the modern recommended algorithm
  -N ''        no "passphrase" (an extra password on the private key, skipped here)
  -f file      where to store it
The private key's permissions must be 600 (only you can read/write) or ssh refuses to use it.
9-16.goal: Generate an ed25519 key pair in ~/.ssh/ (file name id_ed25519) without a passphrase.

hints: Format: ssh -p port user@host command (the command is cat note.txt).
Add -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new to avoid getting stuck on the fingerprint question.
Type: ssh -p 2222 -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new vaultkeeper@127.0.0.1 cat note.txt and answer the content.
9-17.title: ssh: Remote Login
9-17.story:
ssh lets you log in to a remote machine:
  ssh user@host            log in and get a remote terminal
  ssh user@host command    don't log in, just run that command remotely, print the result and come back
  -p port                  choose the port (default 22)
The first connection asks whether to trust the host's fingerprint; adding -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new accepts new hosts automatically.
vaultkeeper's vault is on local port 2222 and your public key is already placed there.
9-17.goal: Use ssh to connect as vaultkeeper to port 2222 on 127.0.0.1, read the contents of ~/note.txt and submit it with answer.
9-17.reveal: There's a note in the keeper's account: "I'm not missing. I'm trapped in an offline node of the star net, and can only call for help through these fragments of signal."

hints: Upload format: scp localfile user@host:remotename
The port needs uppercase -P: -P 2222.
Type: scp -P 2222 -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new local.txt vaultkeeper@127.0.0.1:received.txt
9-18.title: scp: Remote Copy
9-18.story:
scp "copies files" between two computers over SSH. It works like cp, except the remote location is written "user@host:path" (after the colon is the remote path; if omitted it's the other side's home directory).
  scp localfile user@host:remotename     upload
  scp user@host:remotefile localname     download
Careful: scp's port option is uppercase -P, while ssh's is lowercase -p.
9-18.goal: Copy the local local.txt to vaultkeeper's home directory under the name received.txt. (Port 2222)

hints: Write the config with a Here Document: cat >> ~/.ssh/config << 'EOF', paste the 5 lines above, finish with EOF.
Set the file's permissions: chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config
Then: ssh vault cat note.txt and answer what you read.
9-19.title: ~/.ssh/config: Giving Connections Nicknames
9-19.story:
Typing a long -p 2222 -o ... every time is tiresome. The config file ~/.ssh/config lets you give each host an "alias" with preset options, so afterwards you just run ssh alias. The format (one option per line, indented):
  Host vault
      HostName 127.0.0.1
      Port 2222
      User vaultkeeper
      StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new
The file's permissions must not be too loose: chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config.
9-19.goal: Define a host called vault in ~/.ssh/config (HostName 127.0.0.1, Port 2222, User vaultkeeper, StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new), then read the note with ssh vault cat note.txt and submit its content with answer.

hints: To forward local 9600 → the 127.0.0.1:9500 seen from the remote side, write -L 9600:127.0.0.1:9500.
Type: ssh -fN -L 9600:127.0.0.1:9500 -p 2222 -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new vaultkeeper@127.0.0.1
-fN keeps it running in the background. Then verify with curl http://127.0.0.1:9600/secret.txt.
9-20.title: SSH Tunnels
9-20.story:
An SSH tunnel: open a port locally and "forward whatever reaches it, encrypted through SSH," to somewhere reachable only from the remote side. Often used to cross firewalls and use internal services safely.
  ssh -L localport:targethost:targetport loginhost
    -L   set up forwarding (local port → target)
    -N   run no remote command, just keep the tunnel
    -f   go to the background
The internal service listens only on 127.0.0.1:9500 (unreachable from outside), but it's reachable from vaultkeeper's side.
9-20.goal: Set up an SSH tunnel forwarding local port 9600 to 127.0.0.1:9500 (via vaultkeeper@127.0.0.1 on port 2222). Afterwards curl http://127.0.0.1:9600/secret.txt must return the content.

hints: Type: openssl dgst -sha256 firmware.bin
The output looks like SHA256(firmware.bin)= followed by a long hexadecimal string.
Take the first 8 characters of the string after the equals sign and answer them.
9-21.title: openssl: Hashing and Verification
9-21.story:
How do you know a downloaded file wasn't tampered with? Compare its "hash":
  openssl dgst -sha256 file
It reduces the file's content to a fixed-length "fingerprint" (the SHA-256 digest); change a single bit and the fingerprint is entirely different. The publisher usually announces the correct hash, and only if yours matches is the file unmodified.
  openssl rand -hex 16   generates a random key
9-21.goal: Compute firmware.bin's hash with openssl dgst -sha256 and submit its first 8 characters with answer.

hints: Type: traceroute -n -m 5 127.0.0.1
The first output line is a header; each remaining line is a hop.
Count the hop lines (starting with 1, 2, 3…) and answer the total.
9-22.title: traceroute: Which Way Do Packets Go
9-22.story:
A packet travelling from your computer to its destination passes through several "routers" (forwarding devices); each one passed is a "hop". traceroute lists every hop along the way, so when the network is slow or down you can see which section is stuck.
  traceroute -n target     -n don't translate names (faster)
  -m 5                     trace at most 5 hops
For the local address (talking to yourself) the path is very short.
9-22.goal: Trace the route to 127.0.0.1 with traceroute -n, count the total hops and submit the number with answer.

hints: First see where it gets stuck: curl -v http://portal:8088/
Layer 1: getent hosts portal gives nothing → add it to /etc/hosts: echo '127.0.0.1 portal' | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
Layer 2: ss -tln doesn't show 8088 → run start-portal to start the service.
Layer 3: sudo iptables -S shows a rule DROPping 8088 → copy it with -A changed to -D to delete it.
After each fix, curl again; the error changes until it succeeds.
9-23.title: Boss: The Portal Site Won't Open
9-23.story:
The star network sends a signal asking you to open the portal website http://portal:8088/, but it won't open. Network troubleshooting goes "layer by layer", from near to far, eliminating one at a time:
  ① name resolution: does the computer know which IP the name portal means? (getent hosts, /etc/hosts)
  ② service listening: is anything listening on the target port? (ss -tln)
  ③ firewall: is a rule blocking it? (iptables -S)
After fixing each layer, curl again; the error message turns into the next layer's problem, which is a key clue in troubleshooting.
9-23.goal: Make curl http://portal:8088/ succeed in fetching content. Find and fix all three problems: the name portal can't be resolved, no service listens on 8088, and the firewall blocks 8088. (Run start-portal to start the service.)
9-23.reveal: The portal site is back. The first message arrives from the star net: "I'm Vega. Thank you for not giving up on Warden. I'm on my way back."
