10-01.title: nano: A Simple, Friendly Editor
10-01.story:
A new chapter. Vega put the station's settings into a repository, and to read and change them you must first be able to use a "text editor" (a program for editing files inside the terminal, with no mouse and no menus).

nano is the friendliest for beginners: the bottom of the screen lists all the shortcuts, where ^ means the Ctrl key:
  Ctrl-O   save (it asks for the file name; just press Enter to confirm)
  Ctrl-X   exit
  Ctrl-W   search
Move the cursor with the arrow keys and type to edit, much like an ordinary notepad.
10-01.goal: Open the file with nano config.txt, change port=80 to port=8080, save and exit.

hints: Type nano motd.txt; a blank editing screen opens.
Just type: Kernel-7 online
Press Ctrl-O, Enter to save, then Ctrl-X to exit. Check with cat motd.txt.
10-02.title: nano: Creating a New File
10-02.story: nano filename: if the file doesn't exist it's treated as "create a new file" and opens a blank screen; it's only really written to disk when you save (Ctrl-O). Handy for short scripts and notes, and easier to fix than cat > file << EOF.
10-02.goal: Create motd.txt with nano, containing just one line: Kernel-7 online

hints: Type vim config.txt and use the arrow keys to put the cursor on safe in the mode=safe line.
Simplest: press i for Insert mode, delete safe with Backspace, type fast, then press Esc to return to Normal mode.
Type :wq (colon then wq) and press Enter to save and quit.
10-03.title: vim: The Art of Modes
10-03.story:
vim is the editor found on almost every server. It's powerful but confusing at first, because it has "modes":
  Normal mode   the state when you open a file; keys are "commands" (move, delete...), not typing. Press Esc any time to return here
  Insert mode   enter from Normal mode with i; only now can you type, and the bottom left shows -- INSERT --
  Command line  begin in Normal mode with a colon :
     :w save   :q quit   :wq save and quit   :q! quit discarding changes

Safe routine for beginners: open the file → press i → edit the text → press Esc → type :wq and Enter.
10-03.goal: Open the file with vim config.txt, change mode=safe to mode=fast, save and exit.

hints: Type vim tasks.txt (right after opening you're in Normal mode).
Type 3G (the digit 3 then capital G) to jump to line 3, then press dd to delete the whole line. If you delete the wrong one, press u to undo.
Type :wq then Enter to save and quit.
10-04.title: vim: Deleting and Moving
10-04.story:
vim's power lies in "combining actions". These are all pressed in "Normal mode" (no need for Insert mode):
  h j k l    left down up right (arrow keys work too)
  gg  jump to the start of the file   G  jump to the end   3G  jump to line 3
  dd   delete the whole line the cursor is on   3dd  delete three lines
  x    delete the one character under the cursor
  u    undo
Save after deleting: :wq.
10-04.goal: Line 3 of tasks.txt is a cancelled task. Delete line 3 with vim, then save and exit.

hints: Type vim log.txt, then press G (capital) to jump to the last line.
Press o to open a new line below and enter Insert mode, type: mission complete, then press Esc.
Type :wq and Enter to save and quit. Check with tail log.txt.
10-05.title: vim: Adding at the End
10-05.story:
There are several ways into Insert mode (all pressed in Normal mode):
  i   start typing before the cursor      a   after the cursor
  o   open a new line BELOW the current one and start typing      O   open one above
  A   jump to the end of this line and start typing
To add a line at the end of a log, the most common is: press G to jump to the end, then o.
10-05.goal: Add a last line to log.txt: mission complete, then save and exit.

hints: Type vim notes.txt and make sure you're in Normal mode (press Esc).
Enter: :%s/alpha/omega/g then press Enter; every alpha becomes omega at once.
Then type :wq to save and quit.
10-06.title: vim: Search and Global Replace
10-06.story:
In Normal mode vim also has "find" and "replace":
  /keyword    search (Enter jumps to the first; n next, N previous)
  :%s/old/new/g   replace the old string with the new one across the "whole file"
     % means all lines, s is substitute, and g means every occurrence on a line
This is almost the same as the sed 's/old/new/g' you've learned.
10-06.goal: notes.txt has many alpha. Use vim's global replace to change every alpha to omega, then save and exit.

hints: q is quit, and the exclamation mark means force.
To not save, you can't use :wq (w is write/save).
The answer is a colon + q + exclamation mark, joined together.
10-07.title: How to Escape vim
10-07.story:
This is one of the world's most famous questions: "I got into vim and can't get out". Stay calm; the steps are:
  ① press Esc (to be sure you're in Normal mode)
  ② type a colon command:
     :q    quit (only if nothing changed)
     :wq   save, then quit
     :q!   discard all changes and force quit (q = quit, the exclamation mark ! means "force")
What if you've messed up and want to abandon all your changes?
10-07.goal: Write the colon command that "discards all changes and force-quits vim" (including the colon) and submit it with answer, e.g. answer :xyz

hints: Format: tmux new -d -s NAME
Type: tmux new -d -s work
Then tmux ls should show a line like work: ...
10-08.title: tmux: Sessions That Never Disconnect
10-08.story:
When working remotely, if the network drops or the terminal window closes, the programs running in it usually die too. tmux is a "terminal multiplexer" that solves this:
  a "session" lives on in the background; you can disconnect or close the window and it's still there, to be reattached later with everything intact.
  tmux new -d -s work   create a session named work (-d creates it in the background without entering, -s names it)
  tmux ls               list all sessions
  tmux attach -t work   reattach
10-08.goal: Create a tmux session named work (in the background; don't enter it). Confirm with tmux ls.

hints: First create the session: tmux new -d -s ops
Then make it run the command: tmux send-keys -t ops 'touch ~/sent.txt' Enter
Give it a moment (sleep 1), then confirm sent.txt appears with ls ~.
10-09.title: tmux: Sending Commands to a Background Window
10-09.story:
tmux send-keys can "type for you" into a session in the background, as if you were sitting at that terminal:
  tmux send-keys -t session 'command' Enter
-t picks the target, 'command' is the text to type, and the final Enter is "press the Enter key" (not the word Enter). This lets scripts remote-control long-running work.
10-09.goal: Create a background session ops, then use send-keys to make it create the file sent.txt in the home directory (touch ~/sent.txt).

hints: First create it: tmux new -d -s dev
Then split: tmux split-window -t dev
Confirm with tmux list-panes -t dev; there should be 2 lines (two panes).
10-10.title: tmux: Splitting Panes
10-10.story:
A tmux window can be split into several "panes", showing multiple terminals at once, like cutting the screen top/bottom or left/right.
  tmux split-window -t session      split top/bottom (default)
  tmux split-window -h -t ...        split left/right (-h)
  tmux list-panes -t session         list panes, one per line
For interactive use the shortcuts are the "prefix Ctrl-b" then a key: Ctrl-b % splits left/right, Ctrl-b " top/bottom, Ctrl-b arrow keys switch panes.
10-10.goal: Create a background session dev and split its window into 2 panes.

hints: First enter and initialise: cd station, then git init
Put the file in the staging area: git add core.conf
Commit: git commit -m "initial commit" (git log shows the record).
10-11.title: git: Your First Commit
10-11.story:
git is a "version control" tool: it records every change to your files, like save points in a game, so you can return to the past and see who changed what and when. The basic flow has three steps:
  git init               turn this directory into a "repository" (git starts tracking it)
  git add file           put a file in the "staging area" (choose the changes to record this time, like a shopping basket)
  git commit -m "msg"    officially record it (check out), the message describing what changed
git's user name and email are already configured for you.
10-11.goal: Turn the ~/station directory into a git repository, add core.conf inside it, and commit it with the message initial commit.
10-11.reveal: The repository's first commit reads: "Initialize Kernel-7 settings. May it be more reliable than I was." The author is vega.

hints: First enter the repository: cd repo
Type: git status (or the compact git status --short).
The file marked modified (or M) next to its name is the answer.
10-12.title: git status and diff
10-12.story:
git status is the command you'll use most; it tells you the current situation:
  which files changed but aren't staged (Changes not staged)
  which were added to the staging area (Changes to be committed)
  which are new files git isn't tracking (Untracked)
  git status --short   compact: one line per file, M meaning Modified
  git diff             shows exactly what changed (- is a removed line, + an added line)
10-12.goal: The repository ~/repo has three files, only one of which has been modified but not committed. Find it and submit the file name with answer.

hints: First cd repo, then type git log --oneline; the string at the start of each line is the short hash.
If the history is long, filter: git log --oneline --grep="fix reactor"
Answer the first 7 characters of that line.
10-13.title: git log: Browsing History
10-13.story:
git log lists all past commits, newest first. Each commit has a unique "hash" (a long string of letters and digits, like an ID number), and the first 7 characters are usually enough to identify it.
  git log --oneline          one line each: "short-hash message"
  git log --grep="keyword"   only commits whose message contains the keyword
  git log --author="name"    only commits by that person
10-13.goal: The history of ~/repo has a commit whose message contains fix reactor. Find its short hash (7 characters) and submit it with answer.
10-13.reveal: The commit that repaired the reactor was authored by vega, three hours before he vanished. The committer email reads ghost@kernel-7, and the code word ECHO-LIMA appears in the notes too: that ghost account is Vega himself. Even before he vanished he was still working hard to repair this station.

hints: First cd repo, then create and switch: git switch -c feature-x
Make a change: echo hi > new.txt
Stage and commit: git add new.txt, then git commit -m "work on feature".
10-14.title: git branch: Parallel Timelines
10-14.story:
A "branch" is a parallel timeline: you can try new features on it, and even if you break things the main line (usually called main) is unaffected.
  git branch name         create a branch
  git switch name         switch to that branch
  git switch -c name      create and switch at once (-c = create)
Commits made on a branch belong only to that branch.
10-14.goal: In ~/repo create and switch to the branch feature-x and make a new commit on it (any file, any message).

hints: First cd repo, then switch back to the main line: git switch main
Merge: git merge feature-y
Confirm with git log --oneline: feature-y's commit now appears on main.
10-15.title: git merge: Merging Branches
10-15.story:
The feature is finished on its branch and you want to "merge" the result back into the main line:
  ① first switch to the branch that will receive it (main): git switch main
  ② then merge the branch in: git merge branchname
If there are no conflicts, git handles it by itself.
10-15.goal: The branch feature-y already has a new commit. Go back to main and merge feature-y into it.

hints: Enter the repo, switch to main and run git merge feature; it tells you config.ini has a conflict.
Open it with an editor (nano config.ini), delete all marker lines and both sides' contents, leaving just one line: mode=balanced.
git add config.ini, then git commit --no-edit to finish the merge.
If unsure where you are, check with git status.
10-16.title: git: Resolving Merge Conflicts
10-16.story:
When two branches changed "the same spot", git doesn't know whose version to keep and stops for your decision; this is a "conflict". In the conflicted file git leaves markers:
  <<<<<<< HEAD
  (the content on this side)
  =======
  (the content from the side being merged in)
  >>>>>>> feature
To resolve:
  ① open the file in an editor and decide the final content
  ② delete the three marker lines (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) and the content you don't want
  ③ git add the file   ④ git commit to finish the merge
10-16.goal: Merging feature into main will conflict: in config.ini mode is fast on one side and safe on the other. Merge it, resolve the final content to mode=balanced, and complete the merge commit.
10-16.reveal: The two conflicting versions: one is Vega's safe, the other Warden's fast. You chose the middle: balanced. Perhaps that's the third answer they were always missing.

hints: First cd repo and look at the situation with git status.
Put it in the drawer: git stash
Switch branches: git switch hotfix. Then git stash list should show 1 entry.
10-17.title: git stash: Put It Away for Now
10-17.story:
You have half-finished changes you don't want to commit, but must switch to another branch (git refuses to switch because of uncommitted changes)? Use stash:
  git stash        put the uncommitted changes "into a drawer", leaving the working directory clean
  git stash list   see what's in the drawer
  git stash pop    take things out of the drawer and restore them to the working directory
10-17.goal: You have an uncommitted change (work.txt) on main. Stash it and then switch to the hotfix branch. The stash list must have 1 entry and the working directory must be clean.

hints: First look at the Makefile: cat Makefile (see the targets and what they do).
Type: make build
Use ls to confirm app.out appeared.
10-18.title: make: Automating Builds
10-18.story:
make is a veteran tool for automating "builds": you write what to do in a file called Makefile, and afterwards make targetname does it. A Makefile rule looks like:
  target: dependency-files
  <Tab>command to run
Note especially: the command line must be indented with a Tab character, not spaces.
This directory already has a Makefile with two targets, build and clean.
10-18.goal: The directory already has a Makefile with two targets, build and clean. Run make build to produce app.out.

hints: First line of the Makefile: result.txt: input.txt
The second line must start with a Tab: tr a-z A-Z < input.txt > result.txt
Writing with printf avoids Tab mistakes: printf 'result.txt: input.txt\n\ttr a-z A-Z < input.txt > result.txt\n' > Makefile, then run make.
10-19.title: Writing a Makefile with Dependencies
10-19.story:
make is clever: it compares the modification times of the "dependency file" and the "target file", and redoes the work only if the dependency is newer (meaning you changed the input). That's how it "rebuilds only what changed". The form:
  result.txt: input.txt
  <Tab>tr a-z A-Z < input.txt > result.txt
Meaning: result.txt is produced from input.txt; to produce it, run the line below.
Beware: the command line must start with a Tab. Writing with printf avoids Tab mistakes (\t is a Tab, \n a newline).
10-19.goal: Write a Makefile: target result.txt depends on input.txt, and its command converts input.txt to uppercase into result.txt. Then run make.

hints: Format: diff -u oldfile newfile
The old file is old.txt and the new is new.txt (the order matters).
Type: diff -u old.txt new.txt > fix.patch, then cat fix.patch to see it.
10-20.title: Making a Patch
10-20.story:
A "patch" is a set of instructions for "how to turn the old version into the new one", which you can hand to others to apply. It's one of the oldest ways open-source projects collaborate.
  diff -u old new     -u produces a "unified" diff (- is a removed line, + an added line)
  diff -u old new > fix.patch   save the difference as a patch file
10-20.goal: old.txt and new.txt are two versions of the same configuration. Produce the patch fix.patch (diff -u old.txt new.txt) so that applying it to old.txt turns it into new.txt.

hints: Rehearse first: patch --dry-run app.conf < fix.patch and see whether it says success.
Apply for real: patch app.conf < fix.patch
Use cat app.conf to confirm the content was changed.
10-21.title: Applying a Patch
10-21.story:
When you receive a patch from someone, "apply" it to the file with patch, and the file is rewritten according to the patch:
  patch file < patchfile
  patch --dry-run file < patchfile     first "rehearse": only tells you whether it would succeed, without changing anything
Previewing with --dry-run before applying for real is good practice.
10-21.goal: fix.patch is a patch for app.conf. Apply it so app.conf becomes the patched version.

hints: Format: python3 -c 'code' (wrap the code in single quotes).
The code: print(2**64)
Type: python3 -c 'print(2**64)' and answer the long number it prints.
10-22.title: python3: A Pocket Calculator
10-22.story:
python3 is a very popular programming language, and python3 -c 'code' "runs a small piece of code directly" without creating a file, handy as a calculator, for processing text and parsing JSON.
  print(...)   print what's inside the parentheses
  2**10        means 2 to the 10th power (** is the power operator)
Python handles very large integers without trouble.
10-22.goal: Use python3 -c to compute 2 to the 64th power and submit the result with answer.

hints: Create and initialise: mkdir mission && cd mission && git init
Write anything in README.md (echo hello > README.md); the Makefile's test target: test: then a Tab-indented @echo tests passed (printf 'test:\n\t@echo tests passed\n' > Makefile works).
Two commits: first git add README.md && git commit -m "readme", then git add Makefile && git commit -m "makefile".
Finally: git branch release, git tag v1.0, and verify with make test, which prints tests passed.
10-23.title: Boss: Build a Project from Scratch
10-23.story:
The station needs a brand-new "mission" project with version control, an automated build and a release tag. This is your final exam combining the editor, git and make.

Break it into small steps and do them one by one:
  ① create the project directory and git init
  ② write README.md (the project description) and commit it
  ③ write a Makefile (with a test target) and commit it
  ④ create a release branch
  ⑤ mark the latest commit with git tag v1.0 (a tag is like a bookmark, often used to mark release versions)
  ⑥ verify with make test
10-23.goal: Create a project in ~/mission: a git repository; a README.md; a Makefile whose test target prints tests passed; at least two commits; a branch release; and the tag v1.0 on the latest commit (git tag v1.0). Finally make test must succeed.
10-23.reveal: The project went live. In the last commit message you read a line Vega left: "The enemy was never Warden. It was the cleanup schedule I forgot to turn off."

hints: Type: strace -f -e trace=openat launch-sys
There's a lot of noise; strace output goes to stderr, so filter with 2>&1 | grep station.
Find the line ending in ENOENT; the path in the double quotes is the answer.
11-01.title: strace: See What a Program Is Doing
11-01.story:
The final stage. launch-sys fails right on startup and only prints a useless launch failed. The program won't tell, but the "kernel" (the system's deepest manager) knows: whenever a program wants to do anything (open a file, use the network...) it must ask the kernel, and such a request is called a "system call".

strace traces and prints every system call a program makes:
  -f                follow child processes too
  -e trace=openat   show only "open file" actions
A failed open is marked ENOENT (No such file).
11-01.goal: Use strace to find which file under /etc/station/ launch-sys tried to open but failed, and submit the full path with answer.
11-01.reveal: What the program won't tell you, the kernel remembers. Suddenly you understand Warden's situation all along: it kept saying "I'm fine", while the real reason was hidden in system calls nobody was watching.

hints: Type: ldd /usr/bin/ssh
The output is long; filter: ldd /usr/bin/ssh | grep crypto
Each line is "name => path"; answer the name in front (e.g. libcrypto.so.3).
11-02.title: ldd: Which Libraries a Program Depends On
11-02.story:
Many programs don't pack all their functionality inside themselves; at run time they borrow "shared libraries" (extension .so, like a communal toolbox). If a library is missing you see "error while loading shared libraries".

ldd program-path lists which libraries a program depends on and where each was found.
11-02.goal: Use ldd to find the cryptography library /usr/bin/ssh depends on (its name contains libcrypto) and submit its file name with answer (e.g. libxxx.so.N).

hints: Type: strings blob.bin; you'll see the text pulled out of the garbage.
Filter: strings blob.bin | grep STRKEY
Answer the whole key starting with STRKEY-.
11-03.title: strings: Fishing Text Out of Binaries
11-03.story:
Binary files (programs, images...) can't be cat'ed; they print a mess of garbage. But they often contain readable text: error messages, versions, paths, sometimes even a key someone forgot to remove.

strings file pulls out the "runs of printable characters" from a file (-n NUMBER sets the minimum length). Then filter with grep for what you want.
11-03.goal: blob.bin is a chunk of random data hiding a key starting with STRKEY-. Pull it out and submit the full key with answer.

hints: Type: xxd -l 4 magic.bin to see the first 4 bytes.
For a continuous string directly: xxd -l 4 -p magic.bin
Answer those 8 characters (lowercase, no spaces).
11-04.title: xxd: Hex View
11-04.story:
Computers store 0s and 1s at the bottom, which are more convenient to read in "hexadecimal" (0-9 plus a-f, each two digits representing one byte). xxd shows a file as "hex + the matching text".

Many file types begin with a few fixed bytes, a "magic number", like an ID card: just by looking at the start you can tell what the true format is (PNG, ZIP...).
  xxd -l 4 file      look at only the first 4 bytes (-l = length)
  xxd -l 4 -p file   -p prints plain continuous hex without spaces
11-04.goal: The first 4 bytes of magic.bin are this file's identifier. Read them with xxd and submit with answer (8 lowercase hex characters, no spaces).

hints: Format: xxd -r -p inputfile > outputfile
The input is hex.txt and the output is restored.bin.
Type: xxd -r -p hex.txt > restored.bin, then file restored.bin shows what it is.
11-05.title: xxd -r: Restoring from Hex
11-05.story:
xxd -r does the opposite: it restores "hexadecimal text" to the original binary file. -p says the input is plain continuous hex.

It's the old trick for "transporting binary data as text" (a binary file is awkward to paste into a message, but hex text isn't):
  xxd -r -p input-textfile > output-binaryfile
11-05.goal: hex.txt is the hex text of some binary file. Restore it to restored.bin.

hints: First find the path: ldconfig -p | grep libz.so.1; the path is after the => at the end.
Plug the path in: nm -D --defined-only PATH
Add | wc -l to count the lines and answer that number.
11-06.title: nm: What a Library Exports
11-06.story:
"Symbols" are the names of functions and variables in a program. nm lists the symbols in a library:
  nm -D file             show dynamic symbols
  nm -D --defined-only   only those the file "defines itself" (i.e. offers to others)
To learn which functions a library "provides", this is the tool.
To find a library's path, use ldconfig -p | grep name.
11-06.goal: Find the system's libz.so.1 (the zlib compression library; ldconfig -p can show its path), count how many symbols it exports with nm -D --defined-only and submit the number with answer.

hints: First get the PID: pgrep -x hidden-proc
Plug the PID in: tr "\0" "\n" < /proc/PID/environ | grep LBP_SECRET
Answer the value after = (without LBP_SECRET=).
11-07.title: /proc: Peeking at Other Processes
11-07.story:
Each process has a pile of "virtual files" under /proc/PID/ that reveal its inner workings:
  cmdline   how it was started
  environ   the environment variables it carries
  fd/       the files it has open
  status    its status
Note: the variables in environ are separated by "NUL characters" (an invisible separator), so cat runs them together; use tr '\0' '\n' to turn NULs into newlines to read them.
11-07.goal: The process hidden-proc was started with the environment variable LBP_SECRET. Read its value from /proc and submit it with answer.
11-07.reveal: Warden's environment variables include a line: LBP_SECRET. It isn't a password, it's something left unsaid. Every process on this station is quietly telling its own situation.

hints: Type: grep MemTotal /proc/meminfo
The output looks like MemTotal:  16384000 kB; you want the number in the middle.
To print only the number: awk '/^MemTotal/{print $2}' /proc/meminfo
11-08.title: /proc/meminfo
11-08.story:
/proc holds more than processes. There are many system information files:
  meminfo   memory details
  cpuinfo   processor info
  loadavg   system load
  uptime    seconds since boot
Commands like free simply read these files and present them nicely.
11-08.goal: Read the value of MemTotal from /proc/meminfo (in kB, number only) and submit it with answer.

hints: It's just a small file; read it with cat.
Type: cat /sys/class/net/lo/mtu
Answer the number it prints.
11-09.title: /sys: Devices and Kernel Parameters
11-09.story:
/sys is like /proc but presents the kernel's "device model" as a file tree:
  /sys/class/net/   the network interfaces
  /sys/block/       the disks
Each device attribute is a small file; reading it gives hardware information, and writing it (needs root) can even adjust the device.
MTU is the maximum packet size an interface sends at once.
11-09.goal: Read /sys/class/net/lo/mtu and submit the lo interface's MTU number with answer.

hints: comm needs sorted input, so sort on the fly with <(sort file).
In both: comm -12 <(sort crew-a.txt) <(sort crew-b.txt)
Add | wc -l to count the lines and answer that number.
11-10.title: comm and Process Substitution
11-10.story:
comm compares "two sorted" lists and outputs three columns: only in the first, only in the second, and in both.
  -1  hide column 1 (only in the first)
  -2  hide column 2 (only in the second)
  -3  hide column 3 (in both)
So comm -12 means "keep only those in both". Note: the inputs must be sorted first.

<(command) is "process substitution": it uses a command's output as a file, with no temporary file needed. For example <(sort a.txt) is "a.txt sorted".
11-10.goal: crew-a.txt and crew-b.txt are two crew lists (unsorted). Count how many people are in both lists and submit the number with answer.

hints: Both files use the ID (field 1) as the common field, which is exactly join's default.
Format: join file1 file2 > output
Type: join ids.txt scores.txt > merged.txt, then cat merged.txt to check.
11-11.title: join: Merging Like a Database
11-11.story:
join merges two files into one line by a "common field", like a database JOIN: both files have an "ID", so the data with the same ID is joined together.
  join file1 file2   by default uses "field 1" as the common field, with whitespace-separated fields
  -t,                use commas instead
  -1 2 -2 1          use field 2 of file1 and field 1 of file2 as the key
Note: both files must first be sorted on that field.
11-11.goal: ids.txt (ID name) and scores.txt (ID score) are both sorted by ID. Merge them into merged.txt (each line: ID name score).

hints: First generate 1 to 8: seq 8, then hand it to xargs through a pipe.
Type: seq 8 | xargs -P 8 -n 1 slow-task
If you accidentally ran it sequentially first the records will be wrong; type /restart to restart the level (it clears the records).
11-12.title: xargs -P: Parallel Processing
11-12.story:
xargs by default processes things one at a time. Adding -P N lets it "run up to N at once", i.e. parallel processing, which uses multiple CPU cores:
  seq 8 | xargs -P 8 -n 1 command
  -P 8   up to 8 at the same time
  -n 1   each job takes only 1 argument
Eight 1-second jobs take 8 seconds one after another, but only about 1 second with 8 in parallel. It's the simplest way to squeeze out multi-core performance without writing a script.
11-12.goal: slow-task takes 1 second each time and records its finish time in ~/stamps.log. Run slow-task 1 to 8 in parallel with xargs (-P 8) so that the eight records' finish times are within 2.5 seconds of each other.

hints: First find them (without changing): find /srv/audit -perm -o+w
For each found item remove others' write permission: -exec chmod o-w {} +
Full: sudo find /srv/audit -perm -o+w -exec chmod o-w {} +, then run the first command again; it should print nothing.
11-13.title: Security Audit: Find World-Writable Files
11-13.story:
A basic security skill: finding "over-permissive" things. A world-writable file means anyone (including a compromised program) can tamper with it.
  find path -perm -o+w   find files and directories that "others (o) can write (w)"
To fix them, combine with -exec:
  find path -perm -o+w -exec chmod o-w {} +
chmod o-w "removes others' write permission"; the trailing + is another form of -exec that hands many names to chmod at once (faster than \;).
11-13.goal: Some files and directories under /srv/audit are world-writable. Find them and remove "others"' write permission from all (directories too) without deleting anything.

hints: First check the current status: sudo passwd -S mallory (P means he can log in normally).
Lock: sudo passwd -l mallory
Check sudo passwd -S mallory again; the status should become L.
11-14.title: Locking an Account
11-14.story:
When you find a suspicious account, "lock" it first rather than rushing to delete it, because deleting destroys evidence.
  passwd -S account   show the account's status (L = locked, P = has a usable password)
  passwd -l account   lock (l = lock): stops this account logging in with a password
Both need root, so add sudo.
11-14.goal: The user mallory is behaving suspiciously. Lock his account (don't delete it).

hints: To delete the home directory add -r.
Format: sudo userdel -r account
Type: sudo userdel -r intruder, then ls /home to confirm his home directory is gone.
11-15.title: Removing an Account
11-15.story:
The evidence is secured, so it's time to remove the intruder's account.
  sudo userdel account      delete only the account
  sudo userdel -r account   -r also deletes the "home directory and mailbox" (r = remove)
Before deleting, make sure the user has no running processes, or it can fail or leave a mess.
11-15.goal: Delete the user intruder together with his home directory.

hints: The rule is: %ops ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/apt
To write into a file that needs root: echo '%ops ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/apt' | sudo tee /etc/sudoers.d/ops
Set permissions: sudo chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/ops, then check the syntax with sudo visudo -cf /etc/sudoers.d/ops.
11-16.title: sudoers: Least-Privilege Authorization
11-16.story:
Don't give everyone full root power. sudoers can specify precisely "who, as whom, may run which commands". A rule looks like:
  %ops ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/apt
  %ops           applies to the group ops (a leading % means a group; without it, a person)
  ALL            on any host
  (root)         may become root
  NOPASSWD:      without entering a password
  /usr/bin/apt  may run only this command
Rules go in a file under /etc/sudoers.d/ with permissions 440; after editing check the syntax with visudo -c, because breaking sudoers can lock you out.
11-16.goal: Give the group ops a minimal grant: members may, without a password, run only /usr/bin/apt as root and nothing else. Write it into /etc/sudoers.d/ops with permissions 440.
11-16.reveal: Warden looked at the least-privilege rule you wrote and said softly: "So 'able to do anything' isn't strength, it's danger." It voluntarily reduced its own privileges to only the few it needs.

hints: First cat sshd_config.draft to see the settings and their current values.

All three settings change, which you can do with several -e: sed -e 's/^PermitRootLogin.*/PermitRootLogin no/' -e 's/^PasswordAuthentication.*/PasswordAuthentication no/' -e 's/^X11Forwarding.*/X11Forwarding no/' sshd_config.draft > sshd_config.hard
Verify: sshd -t -f sshd_config.hard; no output means the syntax is correct.
11-17.title: SSH Hardening
11-17.story:
An internet-facing SSH is an attacker's first target. Basic "hardening" (making it harder to break into):
  PermitRootLogin no          forbid logging in directly as root
  PasswordAuthentication no   disable passwords and allow keys only (passwords can be brute-forced)
  X11Forwarding no            turn off features you don't use
Each setting is one line in the config. Replace line by line with sed:
  sed 's/^PermitRootLogin.*/PermitRootLogin no/' file
(^ is the line start and .* means "anything after".) After editing, check the syntax with sshd -t -f file.
11-17.goal: sshd_config.draft is an insecure draft. Produce a hardened version sshd_config.hard: PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no, X11Forwarding no, with the other settings kept, and passing the syntax check sshd -t -f.

hints: First group and count: awk -F: '{c[$7]++} END{for (s in c) print c[s], s}' users.txt
Use sort -nr to order the counts biggest first, then head -1 for the top.
Full: awk -F: '{c[$7]++} END{for (s in c) print c[s], s}' users.txt | sort -nr | head -1; answer the shell path on that line (not the number in front).
11-18.title: Advanced awk: Statistics
11-18.story:
awk has "associative arrays" (like dictionaries), so one line can do "group by a field and count", one of the most common data-analysis operations:
  awk -F: '{c[$7]++} END{for (s in c) print c[s], s}'
Broken down:
  -F:           fields are colon-separated
  c[$7]++       use "the value of field 7" as the name, adding 1 to its count each time it appears
  END{for (s in c) print c[s], s}   after reading everything, print each name with its count
11-18.goal: users.txt is a list modelled on /etc/passwd (colon-separated, field 7 is the login shell). Find the shell used by the most people and submit it with answer (e.g. /bin/xxx).

hints: Format: sed -n '/startword/,/endword/p' file
The start word is BEGIN and the end word is END.
Type: sed -n '/BEGIN/,/END/p' station.log > section.txt
11-19.title: sed Ranges and Extracting Sections
11-19.story:
sed's "range" form can extract a whole block from a long document:
  sed -n '/start/,/end/p' file
Meaning: from "the line matching start" to "the line matching end", inclusive (-n with p: print only the given range).
11-19.goal: station.log has an important block that starts with BEGIN and ends with END (both lines included). Extract it and save as section.txt.

hints: ls -S logs lists file names largest first (one per line).
You only want the first three: | head -3
Type: ls -S logs | head -3 > top3.txt
11-20.title: Command Golf: The Three Biggest Files
11-20.story:
One mark of an expert is solving a problem with the fewest characters; not for show, but because it means you truly understand each tool's behaviour. This level is easy, but try to make it short and precise.

Tool hint: ls -S sorts by file size (largest first); then head -3 takes the first three, and > saves them.
11-20.goal: logs/ has 8 files of different sizes. Save the names of the three largest (largest first, one per line) as top3.txt.

hints: Format: time ./scriptname
Measure all three: time ./a.sh, time ./b.sh, time ./c.sh
Compare the real line of each output; the largest is the slowest.
11-21.title: time: Who's the Slowest
11-21.story:
Want to compare the speed of different approaches? Put time in front of a command and, when it ends, it reports how long it took:
  real   the actual elapsed time (wall clock)
  user   CPU time spent in your program itself
  sys    CPU time spent in the kernel
The simplest way to compare performance is to time each approach and look at real.
11-21.goal: The three scripts a.sh, b.sh and c.sh take different amounts of time. Measure them with time, find the slowest, and submit its file name with answer (e.g. a.sh).

hints: Format: od -An -t u4 -N 4 file
Type: od -An -t u4 -N 4 num.bin
Answer the decimal number printed (ignore the leading spaces).
11-22.title: od: Interpreting Binary Values
11-22.story:
Numbers in a binary file aren't text (not characters written like "1234") but are stored directly as bytes. od (octal dump) can "interpret" them in a chosen format:
  -An        don't show offsets (the address column on the left)
  -t u4      interpret as "4-byte unsigned integers" (u = unsigned, 4 = 4 bytes)
  -N 4       read only the first 4 bytes
(hexdump -C shows hexadecimal and text side by side.)
"Little-endian" means the low-order byte comes first; common computers (x86, ARM) are little-endian, and od by default interprets in the machine's own order.
11-22.goal: The first 4 bytes of num.bin are a little-endian 32-bit integer. Interpret it with od and submit the decimal number with answer.

hints: ① Find the largest file: sudo ls -lS /var/log/station; empty it but keep the file: sudo truncate -s 0 /var/log/station/audit.log
② Find the CPU hog: ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head, then pkill cpu-hog.
③ systemctl status gateway, journalctl -u gateway: usually a config path off by one letter. After fixing the unit file (under /etc/lbp-systemd/, needs sudo), sudo systemctl start gateway.
④ sudo chgrp ops /srv/shared && sudo chmod 2775 /srv/shared
⑤ Service up but still unreachable? sudo iptables -S, find the rule blocking 9700, change its -A to -D to delete it, then curl http://127.0.0.1:9700/.
11-23.title: Final Boss: The Whole Station Is Broken
11-23.story:
Alarms ring through Kernel-7. Vega's return signal is about to arrive, but five faults have hit the station at once: the disk is stuffed by a runaway log, the CPU is eaten up, the gateway service won't start, a shared directory's permissions are a mess, and the firewall blocks the gateway's port.

You've learned how to handle every one; this is the last battle. Take them one by one, confirming each fix:
  ① disk full → find the big file and empty it
  ② CPU maxed → find and end the CPU-hogging process
  ③ broken service → systemctl status / journalctl for the cause
  ④ messy permissions → chgrp + chmod (setgid)
  ⑤ network blocked → ss, iptables
11-23.goal: Fix everything: ① /var/log/station/audit.log has ballooned; empty it (keep the file). ② End the CPU-hogging cpu-hog. ③ Get gateway.service running. ④ /srv/shared must be writable by group ops and new files must automatically belong to ops (group ops, permissions 2775). ⑤ Make curl http://127.0.0.1:9700/ return GATEWAY-OK.
11-23.reveal: The station fell quiet. Vega's signal appeared on the screen: "Kernel-7, I'm back." Warden replied: "Welcome home, Vega. I've learned how to stand a proper watch." That night, every light on the station came on. You're no longer a newcomer: you're this station's administrator. (Pip whispers: there's still something in /var/lib/ghost you haven't read.)

hints: First see which files there are and what one looks like: ls /var/lib/ghost, then cat one of them.
Pull out all the fragment lines at once: grep -h '^fragment' /var/lib/ghost/*.log (-h hides file names).
Strip the prefix: | sed 's/.*: //' (keeps only the word after the colon); then turn newlines into spaces: | tr '\n' ' '
Finally answer the whole sentence (the extra trailing space can be dropped).
11-24.title: Hidden Epilogue: Vega's Recording
11-24.story:
The station's lights are all on. But Pip notices the directory /var/lib/ghost: it holds 11 logs you never read along the way, left by the ghost account around the time Vega vanished. Each ends with a line "fragment NUMBER: word". Put the words together in order and you get what he wanted to say.

This level is hidden; if you don't want to do it, just /skip.
What to do: pull one line out of each of the 11 files → strip the prefix and keep only the word → join the 11 lines into one.
11-24.goal: Read the fragment word from each of the 11 logs in /var/lib/ghost, join them in file order with spaces into one sentence, and submit it with answer (e.g. answer WORD1 WORD2 ...).
11-24.reveal: The sentence was: "I forgot to turn off the cleanup schedule, but Warden stayed." From the beginning Vega knew who was really to blame. He wasn't hiding from you; he just couldn't face his own oversight. Pip said softly: "I was waiting for you to ask me 'who are you'. I was the first one in the terminal, and later it was you who gave this station a watch officer."
